title: BASIN: Background-Anchored Signal Normalization with Integrated Quality Control for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag
summary: Spike-in-free normalization for CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag when a perturbation changes the overall level of a chromatin mark. BASIN treats reproducible peak-like background in IgG controls as an internal reference, derives per-sample scale factors from it, and includes a QC step that tests whether the normalization assumptions hold. It stayed stable over a >100-fold range of cell input and picked up the global H3K36me3 loss in Drosophila Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization hid; a ready-made anchor panel is provided for Drosophila.
abstract: Quantitative comparison of CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag datasets is complicated when a perturbation changes the global abundance of the profiled chromatin feature or when there is substantial variability between replicates. Read-depth normalization removes global differences by design, whereas exogenous spike-in normalization can introduce substantial technical variability. We developed Background-Anchored SIgnal Normalization (BASIN), an endogenous-reference framework that exploits recurrent, peak-like background in IgG controls as a quantitative internal reference. BASIN Anchor Regions (BARs) act as reproducible read sinks whose representation rises as specific signal falls, allowing global differences to be inferred from the balance between specific and nonspecific reads. BASIN comprises three pipelines: OVERTURE identifies and evaluates BAR panels, HARMONY derives and applies robust sample-specific scale factors from trimmed BAR signal, and CODA determines whether the assumptions supporting normalization are satisfied. BASIN provides a validated, ready-to-use universal BAR panel for Drosophila melanogaster, and the OVERTURE pipeline enables BAR panel development in other organisms. We tested BASIN against independent expectations and compared its performance with spike-in normalization. BASIN remained quantitatively stable across a >100-fold cell-input titration and detected global depletion of H3K36me3 in Set2 mutants that read-depth normalization concealed. BASIN also preserved expected H3K9me3 differences even when target signal overlapped anchor regions. Applied to a variety of profiling experiments, CODA distinguished normalization failures arising from both biological and technical causes. BASIN thus converts reproducible background from a nuisance signal into an internal reference standard, enabling spike-in-free quantification of global chromatin changes while providing an explicit framework to test when and why that normalization can or cannot be trusted.

title: Combining family history, polygenic scores, and childhood trauma to predict major depressive disorder
summary: Asks whether adding family history of psychiatric disorders, multi-trait polygenic scores, childhood trauma and background factors together predicts lifetime major depression better than any subset of them. Elastic net and XGBoost models were trained and cross-validated in GLAD+ (about 14k people) and UK Biobank (about 111k). The combined models reached AUC 0.83 in GLAD+ and 0.74 in UK Biobank, held up in external validation, and family history and trauma each predicted better than the polygenic scores.
abstract: Objective: Risk stratification for major depressive disorder (MDD) remains limited by clinical heterogeneity and modest genomic prediction. We examined whether integrating family history, polygenic risk scores (PRS), childhood trauma, and background factors improves prediction of lifetime MDD diagnosis and its severity, relative to models including only subsets of these predictors. Methods: Analyses included 9,927 cases and 4,452 controls from the Genetic Links to Anxiety and Depression Study and NIHR BioResource (GLAD+) and 40,667 cases and 70,755 controls from UK Biobank (UKB). Lifetime MDD was defined using DSM-5 based online assessments. Predictors included family history of multiple psychiatric disorders (mFH), multi-trait PRSs (mPRS), childhood trauma, and background factors (sex and ten genetic principal components). Nested elastic net regression and XGBoost were used to predict MDD within and across cohorts. Results: Multivariable models integrating mFH, mPRS, childhood trauma, and background factors demonstrated strong risk classification (AUC=0.83 in GLAD+; 0.74 in UKB). Family history consistently outperformed multi-trait PRS (GLAD+: 0.74 vs. 0.66; UKB: 0.65 vs. 0.60). External validation showed preserved classification (AUC=0.71-0.82), with attenuation reflecting differences in case severity across cohorts. Models explained up to 27% of the variance in the number of depressive episodes. Conclusions: Multivariable integration of familial, environmental, and genetic factors yields robust and transferable prediction of MDD. Family history and childhood trauma consistently outperform current PRS for both case classification and severity prediction, underscoring the continued importance of integrating clinical data into prediction models in the genomic era.

title: Cross- species developmental multiomics identifies RHOJ as a regulator of human-enriched cortical progenitor states
summary: Compares time-resolved paired snRNA/snATAC profiles of human, macaque and mouse fetal cortex and finds human-enriched outer radial glia programs that include the gene RHOJ. An intronic RHOJ enhancer drives more reporter activity with the human sequence than with other primate versions, partly because of a human-specific change in an AP-1 motif. Deleting the enhancer in human cortical organoids lowered RHOJ expression and impaired organoid growth and progenitor composition.
abstract: Expansion of the primate cerebral cortex is associated with increased proliferation and diversification of neural progenitors, particularly outer radial glia (oRG), but the evolutionary developmental changes underlying these features remain unclear. Here, we integrate time-resolved, paired single-nucleus transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiles from human, macaque and mouse fetal cortex to compare their radial glial developmental programs. Developmental alignment within a conserved corticogenic framework identified two human-enriched programs associated with oRG features and progenitor maintenance. We identified RHOJ, which encodes a conserved small GTPase, as an oRG-enriched gene with elevated expression in human cortex. Ectopic RHOJ expression in mouse fetal cortex increased the proportions of neural progenitors and cells with oRG-like morphology, and altered the relative abundance of SATB2+ and TBR1+ neuronal populations. An intronic RHOJ enhancer showed greater reporter activity for the human sequence than for orthologous non-human primate sequences, partly attributable to a human-specific substitution within a predicted AP-1 binding motif. In human cortical organoids, deletion of this enhancer reduced RHOJ expression, impaired organoid growth and altered progenitor and neuronal populations. These findings link human-enriched developmental programs to evolutionary modification of progenitor properties, supporting altered deployment of conserved genes as a potential contributor to cortical progenitor diversification.

title: Fixed group shrinkage exposes the fairness accuracy Pareto frontier for cross ancestry polygenic risk scores
summary: Introduces cluster_fixed, a shrinkage framework that uses ancestry labels to trace the whole trade-off curve between overall PRS accuracy and the accuracy gap between populations, instead of returning one optimized model. In 1000 Genomes simulations and Pan-UK Biobank height effects it cut the worst-case subgroup disparity by roughly 50-72%, usually at a cost in overall accuracy, though both can improve when population-specific effects are large. Other correction strategies did not match its fairness gains.
abstract: Background: Cross-ancestry polygenic risk scores (PRS) show marked prediction heterogeneity across populations. Existing polygenic prediction pipelines produce only one optimized model and cannot quantify achievable prediction accuracy under predefined limits on performance imbalance across population subgroups. We introduce a fixed-group shrinkage framework, named cluster_fixed, which uses known ancestry labels to map the Pareto frontier between prediction accuracy and cross-population fairness. Results: Using genotypes from the 1000 Genomes project and simulated phenotypes, we varied the relative contributions of population-specific and shared genetic effects. When genetic effects are mostly shared across groups, cluster_fixed reduced the worst-case subgroup prediction disparity by 71.7%, with a 57.8% drop in global prediction accuracy (10 random replicates; p < 10⁻⁵). This trade-off depends on the relative magnitude of population-specific genetic effects, and a regime with simultaneous gains in fairness and accuracy appears when population-specific effects are large. We replicated this pattern using height genetic effect estimates from the Pan-UK Biobank, with disparity reductions of 50.5–70.3% on chromosomes 1 and 21. In an independent validation with Pan-UKB β fixed as shared truth and disjoint train/validation individuals, the same fairness-accuracy trade-off was reproduced on both chromosomes (Δfairness = − 0.42 and − 0.37; Δoverall = − 0.055 and − 0.138; all 10 seeds negative, p < 0.01). Competing correction strategies could not achieve comparable fairness improvements. Conclusions: This framework enables the construction of constraint-aware polygenic risk scoring models under chosen subgroup disparity limits. It reveals a full family of candidate models instead of a single optimal estimate, supporting practical decision-making for multi-ancestry risk prediction. Further testing across different human traits and cohorts will clarify real-world utility.

title: From benchmarking to application: a scalable mitochondrial DNA analysis and variant identification framework for whole-genome sequencing
summary: The authors benchmarked four mtDNA variant callers (MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity, mtDNA-Server 2) on 1000 Genomes data and simulations. MitoHPC and mtSwirl performed best overall, especially in non-European haplogroups. Based on MitoHPC they built MARVel, a reproducible workflow with QC reports, interactive variant curation and an mtDNA PCA reference, and it recovered known pathogenic variants in an ataxia cohort.
abstract: Purpose: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants are implicated in a wide range of diseases. The increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing enables mtDNA analysis in large-scale clinical and population studies. However, optimal tools for accurate variant detection from short-read data remain unclear. Methods: We systematically benchmarked four scalable mtDNA variant calling tools: MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity, and mtDNA-Server 2. Using 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) data and simulations across diverse haplogroups, we evaluated performance in detecting homoplasmic and heteroplasmic variants. Using the optimal tool, we built MARVel (https://github.com/bahlolab/MARVel), an integrated workflow combining variant calling, automated quality-control reporting, and interactive variant curation, including an mtDNA principal component reference from 1KG that captures haplogroup structure and enables projection of external cohorts. We then applied MARVel to an independent ataxia cohort to assess research utility. Results: MitoHPC and mtSwirl showed the strongest overall performance, particularly in non-European populations, with MitoHPC preferred for its ease of implementation. mity excelled in detecting low variant allele frequency single nucleotide variants (SNVs) but underperformed for insertions/deletions and showed inconsistent multi-nucleotide polymorphism normalisation. mtDNA-Server 2 maximised SNV sensitivity but had a higher false-positive rate and missed variants in the MT-RNR2 region. Applying MARVel (MitoHPC) to the ataxia cohort recovered known pathogenic mtDNA variants and identified additional candidates for investigation. Conclusion: We provide guidance for mtDNA tool selection in large-scale sequencing studies, along with a reproducible benchmarking framework for future evaluation as methods evolve. We also developed MARVel to facilitate disease-associated mtDNA variant discovery and reporting, supporting robust and scalable mtDNA analysis.

title: Genetic analysis of non-familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease patients
summary: The authors compared 87 sporadic early-onset Alzheimer's cases with late-onset cases and ADSP controls using GWAS, SKAT gene tests, polygenic scores and a rare-variant review of known AD genes. The only strong signals were at the APOE locus. Early-onset cases did not carry extra rare variants in APP, PSEN1, PSEN2 or modifier genes and had intermediate polygenic risk, which suggests their genetics overlap with late-onset AD.
abstract: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), defined by symptom onset before age 65, can be either familial or sporadic and accounts for approximately 5% of all Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases, with only approximately 10% showing Mendelian inheritance. In this study, we compare the genetic architecture of four cohorts comprising 87 sporadic EOAD cases, 1,018 late-onset AD (LOAD) cases, 585 non-demented controls (TGEN2-AD and TGEN2-ND cohorts), and 3,487 non-demented controls from the AD Sequencing Project (ADSP-CTL). We observed a significant enrichment of the APOE epsilon 4 allele in the EOAD cohort compared to controls (52.2% vs 20.1%; p = 1.54e-10), although its frequency was lower than in the LOAD cohort (64.5%; p = 0.0298). As expected, APOE epsilon 4 was strongly enriched in the LOAD group relative to controls (p = 1.23e-63). Sporadic EOAD genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis and sequence kernel association tests (SKAT) confirmed strong association signals in the APOE locus, including the genes APOE, APOC1, NECTIN2, and TOMM40. AD-related polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis showed that EOAD patients carried an intermediate genetic risk (mean PRS = 40.1), significantly lower than LOAD (mean PRS = 57.5; p = 6.7e-05) but higher than controls (mean PRS = 25.1; p = 6.1e-04). Notably, rare variants in autosomal dominant AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and previously reported EOAD/LOAD modifier genes were not enriched in the sporadic EOAD cohort. These results suggest that, despite earlier onset, sporadic EOAD is not driven by a higher polygenic burden or rare high-impact variants. Instead, its genetic architecture appears to overlap more closely with LOAD, supporting the hypothesis that EOAD may represent an early and more severe manifestation of LOAD or a genetically distinct subtype. Unidentified risk factors, such as epigenetic modifications or complex structural variants, may contribute to EOAD genetic risk and warrant further investigation to better elucidate the complex genetic architecture of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
summary: Benchmarks six genomic foundation models, plus GPN-Star and AlphaGenome native scores, on about 7,000 ClinVar SNVs in ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy genes. It compares frozen embeddings, supervised fine-tuning and different context lengths. Evo2 was the strongest of the six (AUROC up to 0.96 with 501-bp context), and GPN-Star and AlphaGenome native scores reached even higher MCC; longer context helped most models.
abstract: Genomic foundation models learn representations from DNA sequence, although their usefulness for variant classification depends on the architecture and downstream evaluation procedure. We compared six genomic foundation models using 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants from ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD)-associated genes, with 4,866 variants assigned to training and 2,094 to held-out testing. The analyses included frozen alternate-minus-reference embeddings at 101, 201 and 501 bp, supervised adaptation at 101 bp, and gene-held-out downstream classifier training. GPN-Star V100 and AlphaGenome Atlas AVI were evaluated separately using their native scores. At 101 bp, frozen Evo2 achieved the highest discrimination among the six foundation models (MCC 0.644; AUROC 0.879; AUPRC 0.818). Supervised adaptation increased MCC for three architectures and reduced it for the remaining three. Extending sequence context to 501 bp improved all three primary metrics in five of six frozen architectures, with Evo2 reaching an MCC of 0.864, AUROC of 0.964 and AUPRC of 0.952. Evo2 also led the frozen gene-held-out readouts (pooled MCC 0.641; AUROC 0.852; AUPRC 0.789). GPN-Star V100 and AVI achieved MCC values of 0.929 and 0.938, respectively, using distinct biological inputs and scoring procedures. The number of variants misclassified across all evaluated configurations decreased from five under the original 101-bp readouts to one after including longer contexts and native scores. An exploratory HGVS-category control identified substantial annotation-associated structure in the benchmark labels. The findings characterize classification performance against aggregate ClinVar labels within LGMD-associated genes. Disease-specific pathogenicity and clinical diagnostic utility remain untested.

title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
summary: Builds a TF-enhancer-gene network for triple-negative breast cancer by combining public enhancer-targeting CRISPRi Perturb-seq data from MDA-MB-231 cells with ENCODE TF ChIP-seq binding priors. On held-out CRISPRi results it predicts regulatory links much better than GENIE3 or co-expression (AUPRC about 0.87 versus 0.63-0.68). Central regulators such as CTCF, EP300, MYC and AP-1 factors were prioritized and their signatures were associated with survival.
abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

title: Meta-analysis of Sequencing Data Identifies Candidate Endometrial Cancer Susceptibility Genes
summary: The authors ran gene-level burden tests on rare protein-truncating and deleterious missense variants in 2,675 endometrial cancer cases and about 160,000 controls, meta-analysing UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. They recovered MSH6, MLH1, MSH2 and PTEN with large relative risks. They also report 19 more exome-wide significant genes from the PTV analysis (including PHKG2) and 8 from the missense analysis as candidates that still need replication.
abstract: Background: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in high-income countries, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. While pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes are well-established contributors, the role of rare variants in other genes has not been systematically characterized. Methods: We evaluated associations between rare genetic variants and endometrial cancer risk based on 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from the UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. Gene-level associations were assessed using burden tests, with protein-truncating variants (PTVs) and missense variants (MSVs) predicted to be deleterious analysed separately. Results: Endometrial cancer (EC) risk associations were observed for three established EC susceptibility genes in the rare PTV analysis: MSH6 (RR = 36.6, 95% CI 25.9-51.8), MLH1 (RR = 52.5, 95% CI 21.3-129.4) and MSH2 (RR = 13.0, 95% CI 6.0-28.2). In the rare MSV analysis, PTEN was also significantly associated with EC risk (RR = 9.7, 95% CI 4.0-23.7). Beyond these established susceptibility genes, exome-wide significance was observed for 19 additional genes in the PTV analysis, including PHKG2 (RR = 29.8, 95% CI 9.6-92.8), and eight additional genes in the MSV analysis. Conclusion: This study identifies novel candidate genes associated with endometrial cancer risk, providing a foundation for future replication studies.

title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
summary: Few workflows exist for analysing HIV-1 drug-resistance data from Nanopore sequencing. NanoHIV-DR is a Nextflow pipeline that goes from raw POD5 files to consensus building, then interprets resistance with Sierra and also detects resistance mutations at the read level, below the consensus. It writes clinician-readable reports linked to sample metadata, so users need less bioinformatics expertise.
abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing offers a rapid and portable approach for HIV-1 drug resistance (HIVDR) genotyping, but analysis of the resulting long-read data requires multiple bioinformatics steps and currently available nanopore workflows are limited. We developed NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow-based workflow that streamlines the analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequencing data and generation of HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR processes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, read alignment and consensus generation, before identifying resistance-associated mutations and interpreting predicted drug susceptibility. The workflow provides two complementary approaches to HIVDR analysis: consensus-based resistance interpretation using Sierra and read-level detection of resistance-associated variants, enabling mutations below the consensus level to be identified and quantified. Outputs are integrated with clinical metadata to generate human-readable HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR provides a reproducible and accessible workflow for Nanopore-based HIVDR analysis with reduced bioinformatics expertise and manual processing for translating long-read sequencing data into interpretable resistance profiles.

title: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
summary: The authors benchmarked and tuned the Exomiser rare-variant prioritization tool on exomes from a kidney stone disease cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). The tuned pipeline placed 94% of known gold-standard gene-patient pairs in its top five and proposed 62 new candidate genes. They checked these against gene-level rare-variant enrichment in an extended cohort and in UK Biobank, and ABCC6 was the best-supported risk gene.
abstract: Background: The majority of rare diseases are caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene with Mendelian inheritance. In contrast, common diseases typically have complex genetic etiology, ranging from a cumulative impact of many common genetic variants with small individual effects, to fewer rare variants with larger effects, with monogenic forms at the rare end of the spectrum. While unknown prevalence of the monogenic fraction of common diseases and incomplete penetrance make identification of such monogenic forms of common diseases particularly challenging, their diagnosis can be essential for precision medicine. Automated rare variant prioritization tools, such as Exomiser, aid whole exome sequencing-based rare genetic disease diagnostics. However, Exomiser's utility has not been systematically assessed in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases prior to this study. Methods: We evaluated and optimized Exomiser for prioritization of rare pathogenic variants in common disease using a large kidney stone disease (KSD) cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). First, we benchmarked Exomiser's performance across different settings for KSD "gold standard" variants in established KSD genes with Mendelian inheritance. Next, we utilized the optimal pipeline for discovery of novel KSD genes and compared Exomiser's findings with results from gene-level rare variant enrichment analyses in an extended in-house cohort and the UK Biobank. Results: With the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all (94%, N = 48) previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated 62 novel genes predominantly involved in ion homeostasis, which are now available to the scientific community as candidate genes for KSD. Out of these genes, orthogonal approaches also support ABCC6 as a strong KSD risk gene, in line with previous research, providing a proof-of-principle supporting the utility of Exomiser in the context of common disease. Conclusions: This study serves as an example for automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases, which is a key step for precision medicine.

title: Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
summary: Asks how much SNP heritability different polygenic score methods (clumping, LDpred2-inf/auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) actually capture once GWAS estimation error is corrected for, using independent GWAS halves (including a way to split existing summary statistics synthetically). Methods that shrink effects hard give better raw accuracy but worse error-corrected accuracy, whereas LDpred2-inf nearly recovers full SNP heritability after correction. Aggressive shrinkage can also bias associations with other phenotypes.
abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

title: SpliceVarMech: A causal generative framework for mechanistic interpretation of non-canonical splicing variants
summary: Introduces SpliceVarMech, which compares wild-type and mutant sequences, generates possible splice outcomes with discrete diffusion and uses Bayesian inference to give disruption probabilities with uncertainty for non-canonical splicing variants. On a small validated set from male-infertility genes (31 variants) it outperformed 16 splice predictors including SpliceAI. Fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data raised AUROC from 0.72 to 0.84 on 203 held-out variants.
abstract: Non-canonical splicing variants occur beyond the conserved dinucleotides flanking splice junctions and are difficult to interpret because disruption scores alone do not explain splice outcomes or quantify uncertainty. We have developed SpliceVarMech, a causal generative framework in which a dual-stream encoder compares the wild-type and mutant sequences and conditional discrete sequence diffusion generates candidate splice outcomes. We then apply Bayesian causal inference to estimate posterior disruption probabilities with 95% credible intervals. The framework reports the predicted splice mechanism together with sequence attribution maps and an exploratory mapping to clinical evidence labels. On a gold-standard cohort of experimentally validated variants from male infertility genes, Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on 31 variants yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 1.000. We benchmarked 16 individual splice prediction tools on the same cohort, where the highest-performing tool, SpliceAI, achieved 0.619 on its 30 scored variants. Ablation experiments showed that removing individual components reduced discrimination, and a separate evaluation on 54 variants supported the contribution of fine-tuning. In a cross-domain assessment, fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data increased discrimination from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants without architectural modification. We assessed in-sample calibration, and held-out validation remains necessary. These results support further evaluation of paired-sequence generative modeling and Bayesian inference for mechanistic interpretation of splicing variants across disease contexts.

title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
summary: The IGVF consortium built a knowledge graph to support variant-to-function interpretation. It joins 657 MPRA, CRISPR-perturbation and coding-variant assay datasets and predictive enhancer-gene models with public GWAS, QTL, LD and annotation data, giving about 3 billion nodes and 8.6 billion edges that can be queried through a portal, an API and an MCP server. Case studies at type 2 diabetes, liver-trait and coronary artery disease loci show how it resolves likely causal variants, their target genes and whether they act through coding or regulatory changes.
abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://igvf.catalog.org) Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog's utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease. Updated quarterly with open data and software, the IGVF Catalog provides a scalable resource for variant-to-function discovery.

title: The IGVF Data Portal: a repository for insights into genome function
summary: This paper describes the IGVF Consortium's data portal, which holds more than 240 TB of assay and computational results on how genomic variation affects function. The data can be reached through a web browser, an API and agentic tools. The paper summarizes the available data and the design of the portal.
abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) Consortium has utilized a wide variety of assays and computational methods to study how genomic variation impacts function. To support the collaborative efforts of labs within IGVF, and to share the results of these efforts, the IGVF Data Administration and Coordination Center (DACC) has developed a data portal (https://data.igvf.org/) that serves as the repository for all results from the IGVF Consortium and as the source of results that have been integrated into the IGVF knowledge graph. Data generated by the IGVF Consortium, which has reached over 240 terabytes as of November 2026, can be publicly accessed via web browser, or programmatically via API, as well as via agentic tools. Here, we provide a summary of the available IGVF data and an overview of the design of the IGVF Data Portal.

title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
summary: EPIC2 is a statistical framework that finds which cell types matter for a trait by testing whether GWAS signal tracks with cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility in single-cell ATAC data. It accounts for linkage disequilibrium, runs the test at both SNP and regulatory-peak resolution, and merges the two P-values with a Cauchy combination test. It is released as an R package with vignettes and test data.
abstract: Summary: EPIC2 is a computational and statistical framework for prioritizing trait-relevant cellular contexts by integrating genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. It accounts for linkage disequilibrium when testing for association between GWAS association strength and cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility at both SNP and regulatory-peak resolutions. The resulting P-values are combined using the Cauchy combination test. Availability and Implementation: The core workflow is implemented in R, with source code, vignettes, and reproducible test data freely available at https://github.com/LingxuanZ/EPIC2. Supplementary Information: Supplementary material accompanies this preprint.

title: Read&Tag enables antibody-independent combinatorial and multifactorial chromatin profiling
summary: Presents Read&Tag, a CUT&Tag-style method that fuses engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies straight onto Tn5, so no antibodies are needed. It profiles active and repressive histone marks, DNA methylation and elongating Pol II, and works in frozen tissue and low-input samples. Dual-specificity readers only tagment fragments that carry both H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, so bivalency is measured directly, and barcoded complexes read out four chromatin features in a single reaction.
abstract: Genome-wide chromatin profiling methods based on in situ tagmentation have expanded access to epigenomic information but generally rely on antibodies, thereby limiting their multifactorial capacity and the direct measurement of combinatorial chromatin states. Here, we introduce Read&Tag, in which engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies are fused directly to the Tn5 transposase to target specific chromatin features in situ. Read&Tag profiles active and repressive histone modifications, DNA methylation, and elongating RNA polymerase II, with signal amplitude increasing with target abundance and remaining robust in frozen tissue and low-input samples. Because the targeting module is a protein of defined structure and affinity, two specificities can be combined within a single complex. Tagmentation by such a dual-specificity reader requires H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 to be present together in the same chromatin fragment. The co-occurrence of both marks thus becomes a precondition of the measurement rather than an inference drawn from independently measured profiles. Combining barcoded reader-Tn5 complexes with primer-timed signal augmentation enables the measurement of four chromatin features in a single reaction. Read&Tag therefore provides a modular, antibody-independent platform for combinatorial and multifactorial profiling.

title: A Super-Enhancer-Like Element and a Positive Feedback Loop Drive Ultra-High Expression of CCS for Red Pepper Ripening
summary: Explains the extremely high ripening-specific expression of the pepper CCS gene through a super-enhancer-like array of 22 tandem CArG-box repeats in its promoter, split up by MITE insertions. CaRIN-CaTAGL1 activate the gene in a way that scales with repeat copy number, demethylation lifts repression during ripening, and CaRIN forms phase-separated condensates at the promoter within a positive feedback loop.
abstract: The capsanthin-capsorubin synthase (CCS) gene drives red pigment accumulation in pepper fruit through a ripening-specific transcriptional surge. In the pericarp of mature fruit, it is the second most highly expressed gene; however, the regulatory basis for this exceptional activation remains poorly understood. Here, we identified a super-enhancer-like (SE-like) element in the pepper (Capsicum annuum) CCS gene (CaCCS) promoter, composed of 22 tandem repeats partitioned into three groups by two intervening miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) insertions. MITE-associated siRNAs and DNA methylation suggest a potential role for these insertions in CaCCS repression before ripening, whereas CaDML2-mediated demethylation alleviates promoter repression during ripening. CArG-box motifs present in all repeats mediate CaRIN-CaTAGL1 activation of CaCCS in a copy number-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CaRIN binds and stabilizes CaTAGL1, and the resulting heteromeric complex activates the CaRIN promoter, establishing an autoregulatory positive feedback loop that amplifies CaRIN accumulation during ripening. CaRIN further undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation through its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region, forming nuclear condensates that are enriched at the CaCCS promoter and contain CaTAGL1. This study reveals how an SE-like cis-element, MITEs-directed epigenetic dynamics, and a self-reinforcing CaRIN-CaTAGL1 transcriptional circuit and biomolecular condensates work together to drive the ripening-specific increase in CaCCS expression. Our findings reveal the regulatory mechanisms through which quantitative and temporal control of gene expression underlies metabolic innovation in Capsicum species.

title: Brain Cell-Type-Specific X-Chromosome Gene Regulation Reveals Sex-Biased Candidate Genes in Neurodegeneration
summary: The authors mapped X-chromosome cis-eQTLs in seven brain cell types from 423 older individuals and found 212 genetically regulated X-linked genes, most of them cell-type specific and some with sex-dependent effects. Combining this resource with X-chromosome GWAS through TWAS, Mendelian randomization and colocalization nominated 11 candidate causal genes, each tied to a cell type, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy.
abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes (~5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

title: Brain-derived multi-omics prioritization of mitochondria-related genes in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depressive disorder
summary: The study tested mitochondria-related genes for psychiatric risk by running SMR, HEIDI and colocalization with brain methylation, expression and protein QTLs against GWAS of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression. A tiered evidence framework ranked ACADVL and SLC25A24 as the strongest schizophrenia candidates, and ENDOG emerged as a regulatory signal driven by methylation.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in psychiatric disorders, yet the regulatory mechanisms linking brain-expressed mitochondrial genes to disease risk remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we employed an integrative multi-omics approach combining brain-derived DNA methylation, gene expression, and protein abundance quantitative trait locus (QTL) datasets to evaluate genetically predicted associations of mitochondria related molecular traits with schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD), cross-disorder phenotypes, and clinical subtypes. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), Heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) testing, and Bayesian colocalization analyses were applied, followed by a study-specific three-tier framework to prioritize potential putative causal genes. Our analyses prioritized ACADVL and SLC25A24 as Tier 1 genes for SCZ, COX11 as a Tier 2 gene for SCZ, and DLST, ENDOG, and PDF as Tier 3 genes for SCZ. ENDOG and PDF were also prioritized for the BD-SCZ cross-disorder phenotype. Further SMR analyses across molecular layers supported ENDOG as a methylation-linked regulatory signal, whereas expression-to-protein associations for COX11 and SLC25A24 showed colocalization support but did not meet the HEIDI criterion. Single-cell analyses suggested context-dependent ENDOG effects across immune cell types. Together, these findings support the involvement of mitochondria-related genes across molecular layers in psychiatric disorders and identify genetically supported candidate genes that warrant experimental validation.

title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
summary: CELL-X aims to work out which genes at T2D GWAS loci matter and in which islet cell type they act. It scores 37 genetically supported T2D genes for cell-type specificity and for expression changes across normal, prediabetic and T2D states, using an islet single-cell atlas of about 246,000 cells. Beta cells came out as the main disease-relevant cell type, and known causal genes such as SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK and TCF7L2 ranked highly in a 30-gene benchmark.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

title: Multiancestry genome-wide association and integrative multiomics analyses implicate key pathways in endometriosis
summary: This is the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative GWAS of endometriosis: over 1 million participants, 32% of them of non-European ancestry, with new procedure-confirmed case definitions. It found 58 risk regions, 27 of them new, including loci seen only in African and admixed American groups. Follow-up comorbidity scans and multi-omic analyses pointed to 314 genes as possible drug targets.
abstract: Endometriosis is a painful and heterogeneous condition that affects up to one in ten women. Its genetic underpinnings remain partially unknown, and its precise disease mechanisms are yet to be elucidated. Here we report a genome-wide study of endometriosis as part of the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative representing over 1 million participants (32% non-European ancestry). We detected 58 genomic regions (27 previously unreported) across diverse ancestry groups and new procedure-confirmed case identification algorithms. These include loci unique to African and admixed American populations. A search for genetically driven comorbidities revealed dozens of associations with known and previously uncharacterized risk factors. Then, within prioritized cellular contexts, we found numerous examples of gene expression affected by endometriosis status. Including further multiomic analyses, we implicated a total of 314 genes, suggesting multiple targets for therapeutic intervention. Our findings span molecular, cellular and phenotypic scales, highlighting interconnected pathways that underscore the multifaceted etiology of endometriosis.

title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
summary: Built ten-year survival methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, using reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and an untouched holdout set. Eight scores reached a holdout C-index of 0.80 or higher (including CKD, COPD, heart failure, type 2 diabetes and dementia), with hazard ratios of 2.6-4.1 per SD. Most of these top scores compared favourably with published polygenic and methylation scores.
abstract: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. The methylation risk scores for eight diseases reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80: chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes with at least 50 events each, and interstitial lung disease, dementia and fatty liver disease with fewer. For the five scores with at least 50 events, adjusted hazard ratios per standard deviation ranged from 2.6 to 4.1, with the highest risk tertile containing 73 to 90% of the ten-year events. Panel CpGs were enriched for cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing and sterol metabolism. Against reported values, the eight top-tier methylation risk scores exceed published polygenic and methylation scores alone, and exceed published polygenic and methylation scores that include clinical covariates for seven of the eight diseases (the exception is type 2 diabetes, where our AUC of 0.865 without clinical risk factors is close to a methylation-plus-risk-factor model at 0.872, and our C-index of 0.809 is lower than the C-index for a polygenic-plus-risk-factor at 0.85). These results indicate that a single blood methylation profile can rank ten-year risk for several common diseases at a level that compares favourably with published genetic and methylation scores.

title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
summary: The authors asked whether rare copy number variants (MAF <1%) called from All of Us short-read WGS help explain alcohol use disorder risk. They ran genome-wide, gene-set and region-level rCNV burden tests in about 56,000 participants from European, African and Admixed American ancestry groups and combined them by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. Genome-wide burden and large rCNV regions were not associated with AUD. They found a global protective signal for duplications, a modest risk effect of deletions in a neurodevelopmental gene set, and a significant 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, which suggests rCNVs add little to AUD liability at current sample sizes.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region ≥10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

title: VEGABrain: a Visualizer of Enriched Gene Analysis for the developing human brain
summary: VEGABrain is a web tool that needs no installation. It maps bulk RNA-seq expression onto cortical and subcortical brain atlas surfaces across five developmental windows, from the first trimester to adulthood. It provides precomputed ssGSEA enrichment maps for about 19,000 gene sets and computes maps on demand for gene lists that users upload.
abstract: RNA sequencing datasets are widely reused resources in developmental neuroscience, yet inspecting them spatially remains unclear and difficult. Here, we present VEGABrain, an openly accessible web tool that renders bulk RNA-seq onto brain cortical and subcortical atlas surfaces across five human developmental windows spanning the first trimester to adulthood. Beyond single-gene maps, VEGABrain contributes a composite per-region enrichment layer using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) scores precomputed for ∼19,000 gene sets drawn from Gene Ontology, Reactome, KEGG, BioCarta, the Human Phenotype Ontology and the MSigDB hallmark collection, and aggregated to a score for every gene set, developmental window and brain region. Furthermore, VEGABrain allows users to submit a custom gene list and obtain its ssGSEA map across development, computed on demand. VEGABrain is open source and requires no installation, offering easy-to-query expression throughout development and brain areas.

title: Cellular reconfiguration of Alzheimer’s disease genetic susceptibility across aging and pathology
summary: Asks which brain cell types carry Alzheimer's GWAS risk genes and how this changes with ageing and disease stage. The authors built scGIPA, which combines AD association results, brain regulatory data and hippocampal single-nucleus RNA-seq with in silico perturbation to score each cell type's contribution. Six functional modules shifted between cell types across stages, with lipid-clearance and amyloid programmes strongest in early pathology, and about half of the contributing genes acted in both ageing and pathology, often in the same cell types.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies identify Alzheimer’s disease (AD) susceptibility genes, but understanding how these genetic signals are organized across ageing, disease progression and cell types is a fundamental biological challenge. We developed single-cell Genetically Informed Perturbation Analysis (scGIPA) to integrate AD associations, brain regulatory evidence and hippocampal single-nucleus transcriptomes, resolving cellular contributions and genetic-route dependence through in silico perturbation. Across healthy ageing and early and later pathology, six overlapping functional modules showed stage-dependent cellular configurations; lipid-clearance and amyloid-fibril-regulation contributions peaked in early pathology. Of 1,469 AD-associated genes, 349 contributed to both ageing and pathology, representing 50.2% of participating genes. Genes contributing to both ageing and pathology preferentially retained contributions in the same cell types and were enriched in an external microglial co-expression module. PVR and HBEGF highlighted endothelial ageing, whereas APOE and BIN1 showed changing cellular contributions and genetic-route dependence across stages. Our findings reveal how AD susceptibility is reorganized across ageing and pathology within interconnected vascular, glial and neuronal programmes.

title: Dosage compensation is regulated by segregated chromatin modules during development in Drosophila
summary: Combines sexed epigenomic and 3D genome data from Drosophila embryos to adults to study how X-chromosome dosage compensation is tuned across genes. About 30% of X-linked genes are compensated only in specific stages or tissues. Housekeeping genes compensated in all samples form constitutive long-range contacts with HAS elements at stable TAD boundaries, while stage-specific genes gain contacts with PionX and 1.688 satellite elements over development.
abstract: Dosage compensation (DC) restores the expression balance between the X chromosome and autosomes in males. How this chromosome-wide regulation is precisely regulated to accommodate the heterogeneous functions and dosage-sensitivity among X-linked genes is unclear. To address this, we analyse the epigenomic and 3D genome data of mostly sexed samples from embryos to adults of Drosophila melanogaster, whose DC is known to be mediated by three classes of X-enriched sequence elements of HAS/CES, PionX and 1.6883F satellites. We find that about 30% of the X-linked genes are compensated specifically in one or a few male stages or tissues, indicated by their significant bindings of the DC-associated protein or H4K16ac histone modification. These specifically (SDC) or facultatively (FDC) compensated genes are more likely to have a developmentally regulated expression and a highly relevant function with the stage or tissue where they are compensated. They show a higher level of co-binding of facultative heterochromatin hallmark H3K27me3 than the constitutively (CDC) compensated housekeeping genes. CDC genes preferentially harbor constitutive long-range (>1Mb) contacts (LRCs) with other CDC genes and the HAS elements, which form by the onset of DC in embryos. While SDC and FDC genes show developmentally increased LRCs with the respective type of genes and the PionX elements and 1.6883F satellites. The CDC genes and their interacting partners more often coincide with the constitutive boundaries of topologically associated domains, while the other DC genes tend to coincide with the developmentally regulated boundaries. Our results uncover that the Drosophila DC is regulated through separate chromatin modules between housekeeping vs. developmental genes involving different combinations of regulatory sequence elements and 3D genome contacts. This provides broad implications for the hierarchical regulation of DC against different developmental and gene backgrounds among other organisms.

title: Functionally decoupled cis-regulatory signals at PCOLCE2 link fibroblast-lineage collagen maturation to pelvic organ prolapse
summary: The study asks which cell type and regulatory signal carry a suggestive pelvic organ prolapse GWAS signal at PCOLCE2. It combines fibroblast-eQTL cis-MR, colocalization, CAUSE, stratified fine-mapping, pQTL deconvolution and single-cell data. It finds that the risk acts through a fibroblast-restricted cis-regulatory effect on PCOLCE2 that is separate from a blood signal controlling circulating protein, although the index signal is not genome-wide significant and still needs replication.
abstract: Background. Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a common failure of fibrocollagenous pelvic support. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) report a sub-genome-wide suggestive association at PCOLCE2 (regional minimum p = 2.5×10⁻⁷), which encodes a secreted regulator of procollagen C-terminal processing, but they do not establish which cell type, which molecular species or which regulatory signal carries the risk. Methods. This was a pre-specified study of a five-gene collagen-assembly panel and of one GWAS-suggestive locus, not an unbiased genome-wide screen, and it used public summary-level and single-cell data only; no functional assay was performed. The analysis combined cis-Mendelian randomisation (MR) with fibroblast expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) instruments, colocalisation, the regional causal-inference method CAUSE, stratified fine-mapping across four molecular phenotypes, plasma protein QTL (pQTL) deconvolution, Steiger filtering, a fifteen-endpoint specificity panel, single-cell and pseudo-bulk transcriptomics, and exploratory regulatory annotation. Results. Conditional on the sub-genome-wide index signal set out under Background, genetic evidence supports a triangulated statistical causal inference for a fibroblast-lineage cis-regulatory effect at PCOLCE2 that raises POP risk (OR 1.282 per SD, 95% CI 1.112–1.477), with specificity of this cis-regulatory effect to pelvic-floor endpoints, colocalisation (PP4 = 0.954) and a causal rather than shared-confounding architecture (CAUSE ΔELPD = −7.99 ± 1.64). Within a single haplotype block the locus resolves into two functionally decoupled, statistically inferred cis-regulatory profiles (r² = 0.066); the blood-restricted profile controls circulating PCPE-2 but is unrelated to POP, and every variant that raises plasma PCPE-2 falls significantly below the POP effect predicted by a circulating-dosage model. The fibroblast signal also accounts for the locus's bone-density association, which we read as parallel pleiotropy rather than skeletal mediation. PCOLCE2 was expressed selectively in pelvic-floor fibroblasts, and exploratory, under-powered pseudo-bulk analysis (16 versus 5) placed an observed disease-associated expression increment within ECM-remodelling fibroblasts; there the collagen-assembly module was positively but non-significantly displaced (Hedges' g = +0.45, label-shuffling p = 0.38) and only the inhibitor module reached significance, so assembly-biased matrix decay remains a working mechanistic hypothesis. Conclusions. Conditional on independent POP GWAS replication — the index signal is sub-genome-wide significant and every inference here depends on it — the disease-relevant signal at this locus is a fibroblast-restricted cis-regulatory effect on PCOLCE2 rather than circulating protein dosage. More generally, the locus shows that apparent gene-level pleiotropy at matrix genes can resolve into functionally decoupled, tissue-restricted cis-regulatory profiles within a single haplotype block — a principle that changes how such GWAS signals should be read and followed up.

title: MitoArc: A Reproducible Short-Read Workflow for Human Mitochondrial Genome Analysis with Circular-Coordinate and NUMT-Aware Evaluation
summary: MitoArc is a Nextflow workflow for calling human mtDNA variants from FASTQ/BAM/CRAM. It handles circular-coordinate shifting, NUMT evidence, haplogroups and contamination, and runs Mutect2 and mutserve2 side by side. On 18 synthetic benchmark datasets (100x-5000x), strict mitochondrial mapping removed NUMT false positives at some cost to recall, and GATK recall increased with depth (0.74 to 0.92).
abstract: Human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis from short-read sequencing is complicated by nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), circular-reference coordinates, sequencing depth, and variant-caller configuration. We developed MitoArc, a Nextflow workflow that accepts paired-end FASTQ files or pre-aligned BAM and CRAM files, retains available nuclear mapping context, and performs standard and shifted-coordinate processing. It runs Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) Mutect2 and mutserve2 independently and reports mitochondrial quality metrics, NUMT evidence, haplogroups, contamination estimates, functional annotations, consensus sequences, and reproducibility outputs. We evaluated MitoArc using 18 controlled datasets, spanning three technical replicates and six sequencing depths (100x-5000x), with 648 allele-level truth observations. Requiring confident primary mitochondrial mapping eliminated 33 observable synthetic NUMT-associated false-positive calls but reduced recall from 0.894 to 0.796. In a matched evaluation comprising 108 truth observations, standard-only and standard-plus-shifted GATK processing produced identical variant recovery and allele-fraction estimates. GATK recall increased from 0.741 at 100x to 0.917 at 5000x, while temporary working storage increased approximately 20-fold. Against the complete truth set, GATK recovered 548 observations and mutserve2 recovered 311 under the evaluated configurations; mutserve2 insertion and deletion modes were not enabled. The benchmark used synthetic data without a background sequencing-error model. A reduced HG002 dataset demonstrated end-to-end operation of the pre-aligned workflow, subject to incomplete nuclear context. MitoArc preserves caller-specific evidence and the analytical context needed to interpret mitochondrial variants. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/sarvezh1/mitoarc.

title: Optimizing phenotype scale improves genetic analyses in large-scale biobanks
summary: The authors present SIQReg, which picks a data-driven transformation of a phenotype so that genetic effects are similar across its quantiles. Across 25 UK Biobank traits the default scale was rejected for 24, and most variance-QTL and other nonadditive signals turned out to be artefacts of scale. On the new scale, GWAS loci rose by 11% and polygenic prediction accuracy by 10%, and these gains replicated across ancestry groups.
abstract: Large-scale biobanks have enabled increasingly complicated genetic analyses across thousands of phenotypes. However, studies rarely consider the appropriateness of the phenotype scale, which can drastically affect inference on genetic architecture. Here we introduce SIQReg, which learns a data-driven phenotype scale by minimizing heterogeneity across phenotype quantiles. Across 25 UK Biobank complex traits, SIQReg rejects the default scale for 24. Generally, SIQReg scales lie between default and logarithmic, indicating that traits are neither purely additive nor purely multiplicative. SIQReg improves both nonadditive and additive genetic analyses. It eliminates most nonadditive signals, including 97% of variance quantitative trait loci, indicating that they may be scale-induced, while preserving biologically plausible nonadditive signals. It simultaneously improves power for additive signals, increasing identification of genome-wide association loci and transcriptome-wide association genes by 11% and 13%, respectively, improving polygenic prediction accuracy by 10%, and identifying 50% more high-risk individuals. These gains are replicated across ancestry groups. Our results establish SIQReg as a principled phenotype scale transformation approach that improves genetic analyses of complex traits.

title: PDAC BioPortal: An Integrated Web Resource for Multi-Scale Analysis of Pancreatic Cancer Transcriptomics
summary: PDAC BioPortal is a web platform that brings together pancreatic cancer bulk (TCGA-GTEx), treatment-associated, single-nucleus (~225k nuclei) and spatial transcriptomics. It offers interactive differential expression, enrichment, pseudobulk and spatial analyses, plus an LLM-based natural-language assistant. As a case study it profiles NRF2 redox-network remodeling across disease and treatment contexts.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits extensive molecular heterogeneity and undergoes substantial transcriptional remodeling across disease and treatment contexts. However, publicly available PDAC transcriptomic resources remain fragmented across experimental modalities, limiting the integrated investigation of molecular programs across biological scales and cellular compartments. Here, we developed PDAC BioPortal, an integrated web-based analytical resource for multimodal interrogation of PDAC transcriptomics. The platform incorporates bulk RNA sequencing, treatment-associated transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. It integrates 349 TCGA-GTEx samples, including a primary tumor-versus-normal comparison of 178 PDAC tumors and 167 normal pancreas specimens; a clinically annotated treatment-associated cohort of 55 specimens (GSE225767); a single-nucleus atlas comprising 224,988 nuclei from 43 patients (GSE202051); and spatial transcriptomic profiles encompassing 23,436 tissue spots from five patients (GSE274103). The platform provides interactive differential expression analysis, over-representation analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, patient-aware pseudobulk comparisons, cell-type-resolved interrogation, and spatial gene-expression visualization. It additionally incorporates PDACopilot, an evidence-grounded natural-language interface connecting user queries with structured datasets and precomputed analytical results. Application of the platform revealed distinct transcriptional architectures across disease and treatment contexts. Primary PDAC exhibited prominent proliferation-associated, inflammatory, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related programs, whereas specimens obtained following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) showed prominent mesenchymal, collagen, and extracellular matrix-associated signatures. Comparison of independent bulk and single-nucleus treatment-associated datasets demonstrated significant pathway rank-order concordance, despite limited linear correlation. Focused interrogation of the NRF2-associated redox network revealed broad transcriptional elevation in primary PDAC, involving antioxidant-response, glutathione metabolism, and NADPH-generating genes. Treatment-associated bulk transcriptomes exhibited selective remodeling of individual network components rather than uniform expression changes. At single-nucleus resolution, NFE2L2 expression exhibited cell-type-dependent patterns, with significant patient-level increases in selected vascular, immune, and endocrine populations across the neoadjuvant-treated cohort and reduced expression in malignant epithelial cells in the standard chemoradiotherapy subgroup. Spatial profiling further revealed interpatient variation in NFE2L2 transcript distribution across treatment-naive PDAC tissues, with differences in the proportion of positive spots despite comparatively consistent expression intensity among positive spots. Higher expression of a selected six-gene NRF2-associated signature was also associated with shorter overall survival, providing an exploratory link between redox-associated transcriptional patterns and clinical outcome. Together, PDAC BioPortal provides an integrated analytical infrastructure for investigating PDAC transcriptional programs across complementary cohorts and biological resolutions. By combining interactive bioinformatics capabilities with evidence-grounded AI-assisted exploration, the platform facilitates cross-dataset molecular interpretation and hypothesis generation while distinguishing transcriptional associations from mechanistic evidence.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
summary: Sparrowhawk is a framework that turns computational methods into interactive browser apps that run locally through WebAssembly, so users need no installation, no command line and no data uploads. For genomic epidemiology the authors wrote new lightweight assembly, AMR-gene annotation and taxonomic identification tools. These reproduce or closely match the results of existing pipelines, and the authors show that methods from other fields can be ported quickly.
abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
summary: VPHYL is an R Shiny app that lets non-programmers convert Nanopore 16S classifier output (Emu, EPI2ME wf-16s) into phyloseq or BIOM objects, with automated QC and diversity reports. Its output matched an independent script for all nine classifier-database combinations, and it reproduced the profiles of a published respiratory microbiome study.
abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

title: YAP1-induced super-enhancer rewiring mediates gene-environment-driven malignant reprogramming and metastatic ecosystem formation in head and neck cancer
summary: Uses integrated epigenomic profiling of mouse models and multiregion human HNSCC samples to track enhancer landscapes during tumor progression. Global chromatin architecture stays mostly stable, while YAP1 moves to newly formed super-enhancers with enhancer DNA hypomethylation; a YAP1–PITX2 axis drives partial EMT, fibroblast activation and lymph node metastasis.
abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterized by frequent TP53 mutations, which are insufficient for tumorigenesis and largely undruggable, underscoring the need to define epigenetic mechanisms driving cancer evolution. Here we show that TP53 mutation facilitates YAP1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming, driving epigenetic tumor evolution by hijacking tissue-regenerative programs. Integrated multi-omics analyses of mouse models and multiregional human HNSCC samples reveal that global chromatin architecture remains largely stable during progression, whereas YAP1 dynamically redistributes to newly formed super-enhancers accompanied by enhancer DNA hypomethylation. Mechanistically, YAP1 establishes an IL6-dependent feedforward loop and cooperates with stage-specific transcription factors, including FOXM1, DeltaNp63, and PITX2. The YAP1-PITX2 axis promotes partial EMT, cancer-associated fibroblast activation, and lymph node metastasis, resulting in a fibrotic and immunosuppressive metastatic ecosystem. These findings identify a YAP1-driven epigenetic circuit as a central hub linking environmental stress to malignant reprogramming and highlight a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HNSCC.

title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
summary: With genome assemblies piling up, the authors built a community nf-core Nextflow pipeline for reproducible pairwise whole-genome alignment based on the LAST suite.
