Next-generation sequencing of 15 patient samples, validated in 50 patients including 5 normal/carcinoma pairs, found progressive APA changes: 3′UTR shortening in cell-cycle and RNA-processing genes, lengthening in adhesion and extracellular-matrix genes, linked to higher cleavage/polyadenylation factor expression. qPCR confirmed APA changes in DMKN, PDXK and PPIE.
abstract: Purpose: Alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA) of mRNAs is a phenomenon that alters 3′-untranslated region length leading to altered posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression. Changing APA patterns have been shown to result in misregulation of genes involved in carcinogenesis; therefore, we hypothesized that altered APA contributes to progression of colorectal cancer, and that measurement of APA may lead to discovery of novel biomarkers. Experimental Design: We used next-generation sequencing to directly measure global patterns of APA changes during colorectal carcinoma progression in 15 human patient samples. Results were validated in a larger cohort of 50 patients, including 5 normal/carcinoma pairs from individuals. Results: We discovered numerous genes presenting progressive changes in APA. Genes undergoing untranslated region (3′UTR) shortening were enriched for functional groups such as cell-cycle and nucleic acid–binding and processing factors, and those undergoing 3′UTR lengthening or alternative 3′UTR usage were enriched for categories such as cell–cell adhesion and extracellular matrix. We found indications that APA changes result from differential processing of transcripts because of increased expression of cleavage and polyadenylation factors. Quantitative PCR analysis in a larger series of human patient samples, including matched pairs, confirmed APA changes in DMKN, PDXK, and PPIE genes. Conclusions: Our results suggest that genes undergoing altered APA during human cancer progression may be useful novel biomarkers and potentially targeted for disease prevention and treatment. We propose that the strategy presented here may be broadly useful in discovery of novel biomarkers for other types of cancer and human disease. Clin Cancer Res; 18(19); 5256–66. ©2012 AACR.

title: Optimal Unified Approach for Rare-Variant Association Testing with Application to Small-Sample Case-Control Whole-Exome Sequencing Studies
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics

title: E2F mediates enhanced alternative polyadenylation in proliferation
summary: How is enhanced alternative polyadenylation linked to proliferation? Poly(A)-site deep sequencing of two human cell models, each profiled in proliferative, arrested and transformed states, revealed global 3' UTR shortening and more intronic poly(A) cleavage with proliferation, with a much weaker link to transformation. Genes encoding 3'-end processing factors were broadly upregulated in proliferating cells, partly driven by E2F transcription factors.
abstract: The majority of mammalian genes contain multiple poly(A) sites in their 3' UTRs. Alternative cleavage and polyadenylation are emerging as an important layer of gene regulation as they generate transcript isoforms that differ in their 3' UTRs, thereby modulating genes' response to 3' UTR-mediated regulation. Enhanced cleavage at 3' UTR proximal poly(A) sites resulting in global 3' UTR shortening was recently linked to proliferation and cancer. However, mechanisms that regulate this enhanced alternative polyadenylation are unknown. Here, we explored, on a transcriptome-wide scale, alternative polyadenylation events associated with cellular proliferation and neoplastic transformation. We applied a deep-sequencing technique for identification and quantification of poly(A) sites to two human cellular models, each examined under proliferative, arrested and transformed states. In both cell systems we observed global 3' UTR shortening associated with proliferation, a link that was markedly stronger than the association with transformation. Furthermore, we found that proliferation is also associated with enhanced cleavage at intronic poly(A) sites. Last, we found that the expression level of the set of genes that encode for 3'-end processing proteins is globally elevated in proliferation, and that E2F transcription factors contribute to this regulation. Our results comprehensively identify alternative polyadenylation events associated with cellular proliferation and transformation, and demonstrate that the enhanced alternative polyadenylation in proliferative conditions results not only in global 3' UTR shortening but also in enhanced premature cleavage in introns. Our results also indicate that E2F-mediated co-transcriptional regulation of 3'-end processing genes is one of the mechanisms that links enhanced alternative polyadenylation to proliferation.

title: Topological domains in mammalian genomes identified by analysis of chromatin interactions
summary: Hi-C was applied to human and mouse embryonic stem cells and differentiated cell types to map higher-order chromatin organization at high resolution. Megabase-sized 'topological domains' turn out to be a pervasive feature that limits heterochromatin spread and is stable across cell types and conserved between species. Domain boundaries are enriched for CTCF, housekeeping genes, tRNAs and SINE retrotransposons.
abstract: The spatial organization of the genome is intimately linked to its biological function, yet our understanding of higher order genomic structure is coarse, fragmented and incomplete. In the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, interphase chromosomes occupy distinct chromosome territories, and numerous models have been proposed for how chromosomes fold within chromosome territories. These models, however, provide only few mechanistic details about the relationship between higher order chromatin structure and genome function. Recent advances in genomic technologies have led to rapid advances in the study of three-dimensional genome organization. In particular, Hi-C has been introduced as a method for identifying higher order chromatin interactions genome wide. Here we investigate the three-dimensional organization of the human and mouse genomes in embryonic stem cells and terminally differentiated cell types at unprecedented resolution. We identify large, megabase-sized local chromatin interaction domains, which we term 'topological domains', as a pervasive structural feature of the genome organization. These domains correlate with regions of the genome that constrain the spread of heterochromatin. The domains are stable across different cell types and highly conserved across species, indicating that topological domains are an inherent property of mammalian genomes. Finally, we find that the boundaries of topological domains are enriched for the insulator binding protein CTCF, housekeeping genes, transfer RNAs and short interspersed element (SINE) retrotransposons, indicating that these factors may have a role in establishing the topological domain structure of the genome.

title: The Poly(A)-Binding Protein Nuclear 1 Suppresses Alternative Cleavage and Polyadenylation Sites
summary: Which factors control alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA)? A reporter-based RNAi screen identified PABPN1, and genome-wide APA profiling in human cells showed its loss broadly shortens 3' UTRs through increased proximal cleavage-site use, which in Cyclin D1 weakens microRNA repression. The triplet-repeat expanded PABPN1 that causes OPMD had a similar effect in mouse and human cells by sequestering endogenous PABPN1 in nuclear aggregates.
abstract: Alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA) is emerging as an important layer of gene regulation. Factors controlling APA are largely unknown. We developed a reporter-based RNAi screen for APA and identified PABPN1 as a regulator of this process. Genome-wide analysis of APA in human cells showed that loss of PABPN1 resulted in extensive 3' untranslated region shortening. Messenger RNA transcription, stability analyses, and in vitro cleavage assays indicated enhanced usage of proximal cleavage sites (CSs) as the underlying mechanism. Using Cyclin D1 as a test case, we demonstrated that enhanced usage of proximal CSs compromises microRNA-mediated repression. Triplet-repeat expansion in PABPN1 (trePABPN1) causes autosomal-dominant oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD). The expression of trePABPN1 in both a mouse model of OPMD and human cells elicited broad induction of proximal CS usage, linked to binding to endogenous PABPN1 and its sequestration in nuclear aggregates. Our results elucidate a novel function for PABPN1 as a suppressor of APA.

title: Systematic dissection and optimization of inducible enhancers in human cells using a massively parallel reporter assay
summary: Introduces MPRA, which clones microarray-synthesized regulatory elements with unique sequence tags into reporter plasmids and reads out tag expression by high-throughput sequencing. Over 27,000 variants of a synthetic cAMP-regulated enhancer and the interferon-β enhancer were tested in human cells, mapping functional transcription factor binding sites at single-nucleotide resolution. Quantitative sequence-activity models (QSAMs) trained on the data were used to design enhancer variants with high induced and low basal activity.
abstract: Learning to read and write the transcriptional regulatory code is of central importance to progress in genetic analysis and engineering. Here we describe a massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) that facilitates the systematic dissection of transcriptional regulatory elements. In MPRA, microarray-synthesized DNA regulatory elements and unique sequence tags are cloned into plasmids to generate a library of reporter constructs. These constructs are transfected into cells and tag expression is assayed by high-throughput sequencing. We apply MPRA to compare >27,000 variants of two inducible enhancers in human cells: a synthetic cAMP-regulated enhancer and the virus-inducible interferon-β enhancer. We first show that the resulting data define accurate maps of functional transcription factor binding sites in both enhancers at single-nucleotide resolution. We then use the data to train quantitative sequence-activity models (QSAMs) of the two enhancers. We show that QSAMs from two cellular states can be combined to design enhancer variants that optimize potentially conflicting objectives, such as maximizing induced activity while minimizing basal activity.

title: High throughput gene expression analysis of the inner ear
summary: A critical review of ten years of microarray studies of inner ear gene expression in mice. It covers studies that searched for deafness genes, developmental transcriptional networks and functional miRNAs, along with work on responses to ototoxic drugs, hypergravity and caloric restriction and on networks downstream of deafness genes. Using public GEO datasets, it also shows that data from independent experiments can be combined to gain new insights, as RNA-seq becomes more common.
abstract: The mouse auditory and vestibular epithelia consist of a complex array of many different cell types. Over the last decade microarrays were used to characterize gene expression in the inner ear. Studies were performed on wild type mice to identify deafness genes, transcriptional networks activated during development, or identify miRNA with a functional role in the ear. Other studies focused on the molecular response of the inner ear to stimuli ranging from ototoxic medications to hypergravity and caloric restriction. Finally, microarrays were used to identify transcriptional networks activated downstream of deafness genes. As template-free high throughput gene expression profiling methods such as RNA-seq are increasingly popular, we offer a critical review of the data generated over the last decade relating to microarrays for gene expression profiling of the inner ear. Moreover, as most of the published data is available through the gene expression omnibus (GEO), we demonstrate the feasibility of integrating data from independent experiments to reach novel insights.

title: Selective inhibition of microRNA accessibility by RBM38 is required for p53 activity
summary: A genetic screen for RNA-binding proteins that control miRNA access to target mRNAs identified RBM38, a p53-induced protein whose blocking of miRNA repression is needed for proper p53 function. RBM38 acts selectively by binding uridine-rich regions near miRNA sites and does little to block miR-34a action on SIRT1. In large human breast cancer cohorts, promoter hypermethylation that lowers RBM38 expression was linked to wild-type p53 status.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) interact with 3'-untranslated regions of messenger RNAs to restrict expression of most protein-coding genes during normal development and cancer. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) can control the biogenesis, stability and activity of miRNAs. Here we identify RBM38 in a genetic screen for RBPs whose expression controls miRNA access to target mRNAs. RBM38 is induced by p53 and its ability to modulate miRNA-mediated repression is required for proper p53 function. In contrast, RBM38 shows lower propensity to block the action of the p53-controlled miR-34a on SIRT1. Target selectivity is determined by the interaction of RBM38 with uridine-rich regions near miRNA target sequences. Furthermore, in large cohorts of human breast cancer, reduced RBM38 expression by promoter hypermethylation correlates with wild-type p53 status. Thus, our results indicate a novel layer of p53 gene regulation, which is required for its tumour suppressive function.

title: Cell Type–Specific Transcriptome Analysis Reveals a Major Role for Zeb1 and miR-200b in Mouse Inner Ear Morphogenesis
summary: A new sorting protocol separated newborn mouse auditory and vestibular tissues into their major cell types, and transcriptome profiling of the sorted cells revealed cell-type-specific expression clusters. Computational analysis pointed to transcription factors and miRNAs that set cell identity, especially the Zeb1/miR-200b pathway controlling epithelial versus mesenchymal fate. ZEB1 pathway misregulation in Twirler mice, which have inner ear malformations, suggests a new mechanism behind deafness and balance disorders.
abstract: Cellular heterogeneity hinders the extraction of functionally significant results and inference of regulatory networks from wide-scale expression profiles of complex mammalian organs. The mammalian inner ear consists of the auditory and vestibular systems that are each composed of hair cells, supporting cells, neurons, mesenchymal cells, other epithelial cells, and blood vessels. We developed a novel protocol to sort auditory and vestibular tissues of newborn mouse inner ears into their major cellular components. Transcriptome profiling of the sorted cells identified cell type-specific expression clusters. Computational analysis detected transcription factors and microRNAs that play key roles in determining cell identity in the inner ear. Specifically, our analysis revealed the role of the Zeb1/miR-200b pathway in establishing epithelial and mesenchymal identity in the inner ear. Furthermore, we detected a misregulation of the ZEB1 pathway in the inner ear of Twirler mice, which manifest, among other phenotypes, malformations of the auditory and vestibular labyrinth. The association of misregulation of the ZEB1/miR-200b pathway with auditory and vestibular defects in the Twirler mutant mice uncovers a novel mechanism underlying deafness and balance disorders. Our approach can be employed to decipher additional complex regulatory networks underlying other hearing and balance mouse mutants.

title: Matrin 3 Binds and Stabilizes mRNA
summary: Investigates the poorly understood nuclear matrix protein MATR3, an ATM substrate. MATR3 binds RNA through its RRM2 domain and interacts with RNA-processing proteins in an RNA-dependent way, and RIP-seq found small noncoding RNAs among its targets. Microarrays identified 77 transcripts whose levels depended on MATR3.
abstract: Matrin 3 (MATR3) is a highly conserved, inner nuclear matrix protein with two zinc finger domains and two RNA recognition motifs (RRM), whose function is largely unknown. Recently we found MATR3 to be phosphorylated by the protein kinase ATM, which activates the cellular response to double strand breaks in the DNA. Here, we show that MATR3 interacts in an RNA-dependent manner with several proteins with established roles in RNA processing, and maintains its interaction with RNA via its RRM2 domain. Deep sequencing of the bound RNA (RIP-seq) identified several small noncoding RNA species. Using microarray analysis to explore MATR3's role in transcription, we identified 77 transcripts whose amounts depended on the presence of MATR3. We validated this finding with nine transcripts which were also bound to the MATR3 complex. Finally, we demonstrated the importance of MATR3 for maintaining the stability of several of these mRNA species and conclude that it has a role in mRNA stabilization. The data suggest that the cellular level of MATR3, known to be highly regulated, modulates the stability of a group of gene transcripts.

title: Rare-Variant Association Testing for Sequencing Data with the Sequence Kernel Association Test
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
summary: Single-marker tests have little power for rare variants in sequencing studies. SKAT is a score-based variance-component regression test that checks a whole region's common and rare variants against continuous or binary traits, with covariate adjustment and analytic p values. It scanned 1000 genomes in 30 kb windows in 7 hours on a laptop, outperformed alternative tests in simulations and Dallas Heart Study triglyceride data, and comes with power and sample-size calculations.
abstract: Sequencing studies are increasingly being conducted to identify rare variants associated with complex traits. The limited power of classical single-marker association analysis for rare variants poses a central challenge in such studies. We propose the sequence kernel association test (SKAT), a supervised, flexible, computationally efficient regression method to test for association between genetic variants (common and rare) in a region and a continuous or dichotomous trait while easily adjusting for covariates. As a score-based variance-component test, SKAT can quickly calculate p values analytically by fitting the null model containing only the covariates, and so can easily be applied to genome-wide data. Using SKAT to analyze a genome-wide sequencing study of 1000 individuals, by segmenting the whole genome into 30 kb regions, requires only 7 hr on a laptop. Through analysis of simulated data across a wide range of practical scenarios and triglyceride data from the Dallas Heart Study, we show that SKAT can substantially outperform several alternative rare-variant association tests. We also provide analytic power and sample-size calculations to help design candidate-gene, whole-exome, and whole-genome sequence association studies.

title: Integration of Transcriptomics, Proteomics, and MicroRNA Analyses Reveals Novel MicroRNA Regulation of Targets in the Mammalian Inner Ear
summary: miRNA, transcriptome and proteome profiles of microdissected mouse auditory and vestibular sensory epithelia were combined and analyzed with the FAME algorithm to find functional miRNA–target interactions. Of 157 miRNAs detected, 53 differed between cochlea and vestibule, and some targets appeared only at the protein level, pointing to translational repression. miR-135b was experimentally confirmed to regulate PSIP1-P75 in vestibular hair cells, suggesting it shapes differences between cochlear and vestibular hair cells.
abstract: We have employed a novel approach for the identification of functionally important microRNA (miRNA)-target interactions, integrating miRNA, transcriptome and proteome profiles and advanced in silico analysis using the FAME algorithm. Since miRNAs play a crucial role in the inner ear, demonstrated by the discovery of mutations in a miRNA leading to human and mouse deafness, we applied this approach to microdissected auditory and vestibular sensory epithelia. We detected the expression of 157 miRNAs in the inner ear sensory epithelia, with 53 miRNAs differentially expressed between the cochlea and vestibule. Functionally important miRNAs were determined by searching for enriched or depleted targets in the transcript and protein datasets with an expression consistent with the dogma of miRNA regulation. Importantly, quite a few of the targets were detected only in the protein datasets, attributable to regulation by translational suppression. We identified and experimentally validated the regulation of PSIP1-P75, a transcriptional co-activator previously unknown in the inner ear, by miR-135b, in vestibular hair cells. Our findings suggest that miR-135b serves as a cellular effector, involved in regulating some of the differences between the cochlear and vestibular hair cells.

title: Complex and dynamic landscape of RNA polyadenylation revealed by PAS-Seq
summary: PAS-Seq is a deep-sequencing method that maps poly(A) junctions and quantifies their relative usage across the transcriptome. In human and mouse, 40–50% of expressed genes showed alternative polyadenylation, and the method also captured conserved histone mRNA and mitochondrial RNA polyadenylation. Profiling mouse ES cells, neural progenitors and neurons showed widespread 3′UTR lengthening during differentiation.
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) of mRNAs has emerged as an important mechanism for post-transcriptional gene regulation in higher eukaryotes. Although microarrays have recently been used to characterize APA globally, they have a number of serious limitations that prevents comprehensive and highly quantitative analysis. To better characterize APA and its regulation, we have developed a deep sequencing-based method called P oly( A ) S ite Seq uencing (PAS-Seq) for quantitatively profiling RNA polyadenylation at the transcriptome level. PAS-Seq not only accurately and comprehensively identifies poly(A) junctions in mRNAs and noncoding RNAs, but also provides quantitative information on the relative abundance of polyadenylated RNAs. PAS-Seq analyses of human and mouse transcriptomes showed that 40%–50% of all expressed genes produce alternatively polyadenylated mRNAs. Furthermore, our study detected evolutionarily conserved polyadenylation of histone mRNAs and revealed novel features of mitochondrial RNA polyadenylation. Finally, PAS-Seq analyses of mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells, neural stem/progenitor (NSP) cells, and neurons not only identified more poly(A) sites than what was found in the entire mouse EST database, but also detected significant changes in the global APA profile that lead to lengthening of 3′ untranslated regions (UTR) in many mRNAs during stem cell differentiation. Together, our PAS-Seq analyses revealed a complex landscape of RNA polyadenylation in mammalian cells and the dynamic regulation of APA during stem cell differentiation.

title: Network medicine: a network-based approach to human disease
summary: Review arguing that diseases rarely stem from a single faulty gene and usually reflect perturbations of interconnected cellular networks. It outlines network medicine tools for finding disease modules and pathways and relating apparently distinct phenotypes. These approaches can help find new disease genes, interpret GWAS and sequencing variants, and identify drug targets and biomarkers.
abstract: Given the functional interdependencies between the molecular components in a human cell, a disease is rarely a consequence of an abnormality in a single gene, but reflects the perturbations of the complex intracellular and intercellular network that links tissue and organ systems. The emerging tools of network medicine offer a platform to explore systematically not only the molecular complexity of a particular disease, leading to the identification of disease modules and pathways, but also the molecular relationships among apparently distinct (patho)phenotypes. Advances in this direction are essential for identifying new disease genes, for uncovering the biological significance of disease-associated mutations identified by genome-wide association studies and full-genome sequencing, and for identifying drug targets and biomarkers for complex diseases.

title: SPIKE: a database of highly curated human signaling pathways
summary: SPIKE (Signaling Pathways Integrated Knowledge Engine) is a database of carefully curated interactions in human signaling pathways, with literature references for each interaction and pathway maps drawn by curators. It mainly covers DNA damage response, cell cycle, programmed cell death and hearing-related pathways. The data can be exported in several formats, and a standalone tool supports pathway analysis and dynamic visualization.
abstract: The rapid accumulation of knowledge on biological signaling pathways and their regulatory mechanisms has highlighted the need for specific repositories that can store, organize and allow retrieval of pathway information in a way that will be useful for the research community. SPIKE (Signaling Pathways Integrated Knowledge Engine; http://www.cs.tau.ac.il/&~spike/) is a database for achieving this goal, containing highly curated interactions for particular human pathways, along with literature-referenced information on the nature of each interaction. To make database population and pathway comprehension straightforward, a simple yet informative data model is used, and pathways are laid out as maps that reflect the curator’s understanding and make the utilization of the pathways easy. The database currently focuses primarily on pathways describing DNA damage response, cell cycle, programmed cell death and hearing related pathways. Pathways are regularly updated, and additional pathways are gradually added. The complete database and the individual maps are freely exportable in several formats. The database is accompanied by a stand-alone software tool for analysis and dynamic visualization of pathways.

title: A Pumilio-induced RNA structure switch in p27-3′ UTR controls miR-221 and miR-222 accessibility
summary: Explains why the tumour suppressor p27 stays high in quiescent cells even though its repressors miR-221/222 are abundant: their target sites in the p27 3′ UTR are blocked. After growth factor stimulation, Pumilio-1 (PUM1) is upregulated and phosphorylated, then binds the 3′ UTR. This binding changes the local RNA structure and exposes the miRNA sites, so p27 is suppressed and cells enter the cell cycle quickly.
abstract: Key regulators of 3' untranslated regions (3' UTRs) are microRNAs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). The p27 tumour suppressor is highly expressed in quiescent cells, and its downregulation is required for cell cycle entry after growth factor stimulation. Intriguingly, p27 accumulates in quiescent cells despite high levels of its inhibitors miR-221 and miR-222 (Refs 5, 6). Here we show that miR-221 and miR-222 are underactive towards p27-3' UTR in quiescent cells, as a result of target site hindrance. Pumilio-1 (PUM1) is a ubiquitously expressed RBP that was shown to interact with p27-3' UTR. In response to growth factor stimulation, PUM1 is upregulated and phosphorylated for optimal induction of its RNA-binding activity towards the p27-3' UTR. PUM1 binding induces a local change in RNA structure that favours association with miR-221 and miR-222, efficient suppression of p27 expression, and rapid entry to the cell cycle. We have therefore uncovered a novel RBP-induced structural switch modulating microRNA-mediated gene expression regulation.

title: Major role for mRNA stability in shaping the kinetics of gene induction
summary: Asks how much mRNA stability, rather than sequential transcription-factor activation, shapes the timing of transcriptional responses. Analysis of many expression datasets alongside a kinetic mathematical model showed that fast-induced genes tend to have unstable mRNAs, a strong global anti-correlation. This relationship was weaker for repressed genes, where normally stable mRNAs often dropped faster than transcriptional shut-off alone could explain, pointing to active regulation of decay.
abstract: Background mRNA levels in cells are determined by the relative rates of RNA production and degradation. Yet, to date, most analyses of gene expression profiles were focused on mechanisms which regulate transcription, while the role of mRNA stability in modulating transcriptional networks was to a large extent overlooked. In particular, kinetic waves in transcriptional responses are usually interpreted as resulting from sequential activation of transcription factors. Results In this study, we examined on a global scale the role of mRNA stability in shaping the kinetics of gene response. Analyzing numerous expression datasets we revealed a striking global anti-correlation between rapidity of induction and mRNA stability, fitting the prediction of a kinetic mathematical model. In contrast, the relationship between kinetics and stability was less significant when gene suppression was analyzed. Frequently, mRNAs that are stable under standard conditions were very rapidly down-regulated following stimulation. Such effect cannot be explained even by a complete shut-off of transcription, and therefore indicates intense modulation of RNA stability. Conclusion Taken together, our results demonstrate the key role of mRNA stability in determining induction kinetics in mammalian transcriptional networks.

title: Expander: from expression microarrays to networks and functions
summary: A step-by-step protocol for analyzing gene expression microarray data with Expander 5.0. It goes from data import, normalization and filtering through clustering and network-based analysis. The resulting gene groups are then tested for Gene Ontology enrichment, co-regulation by transcription factors or microRNAs, and co-location on the genome.
abstract: A major challenge in the analysis of gene expression microarray data is to extract meaningful biological knowledge out of the huge volume of raw data. Expander (EXPression ANalyzer and DisplayER) is an integrated software platform for the analysis of gene expression data, which is freely available for academic use. It is designed to support all the stages of microarray data analysis, from raw data normalization to inference of transcriptional regulatory networks. The microarray analysis described in this protocol starts with importing the data into Expander 5.0 and is followed by normalization and filtering. Then, clustering and network-based analyses are performed. The gene groups identified are tested for enrichment in function (based on Gene Ontology), co-regulation (using transcription factor and microRNA target predictions) or co-location. The results of each analysis step can be visualized in a number of ways. The complete protocol can be executed in approximately 1 h.

title: Associating Genes and Protein Complexes with Disease via Network Propagation
summary: PRINCE is a global network-propagation method that ranks disease genes using a scoring function that varies smoothly over a protein interaction network and uses prior knowledge; it also predicts which protein complexes are linked to a disease. In cross-validation on 1,369 OMIM diseases it ranked the true causal gene first for 34% of them, inferred 139 coherent disease complexes and beat existing methods. For prostate cancer, Alzheimer's disease and type 2 diabetes it proposed new candidate genes and complexes.
abstract: A fundamental challenge in human health is the identification of disease-causing genes. Recently, several studies have tackled this challenge via a network-based approach, motivated by the observation that genes causing the same or similar diseases tend to lie close to one another in a network of protein-protein or functional interactions. However, most of these approaches use only local network information in the inference process and are restricted to inferring single gene associations. Here, we provide a global, network-based method for prioritizing disease genes and inferring protein complex associations, which we call PRINCE. The method is based on formulating constraints on the prioritization function that relate to its smoothness over the network and usage of prior information. We exploit this function to predict not only genes but also protein complex associations with a disease of interest. We test our method on gene-disease association data, evaluating both the prioritization achieved and the protein complexes inferred. We show that our method outperforms extant approaches in both tasks. Using data on 1,369 diseases from the OMIM knowledgebase, our method is able (in a cross validation setting) to rank the true causal gene first for 34% of the diseases, and infer 139 disease-related complexes that are highly coherent in terms of the function, expression and conservation of their member proteins. Importantly, we apply our method to study three multi-factorial diseases for which some causal genes have been found already: prostate cancer, alzheimer and type 2 diabetes mellitus. PRINCE's predictions for these diseases highly match the known literature, suggesting several novel causal genes and protein complexes for further investigation.

title: Comprehensive Mapping of Long-Range Interactions Reveals Folding Principles of the Human Genome
summary: Hi-C is a method that captures interactions between all pairs of genomic loci in the nucleus and reads them out by deep sequencing. It was used to map the 3D folding of the human genome at 1 Mb resolution. The map splits the genome into two spatial compartments that follow local chromatin state, and remodeling of these compartments tracks changes in chromatin state.
abstract: The conformation of the genome in the nucleus and contacts between both proximal and distal loci influence gene expression. In order to map genomic contacts, Lieberman-Aiden et al. (p. 289 , see the cover) developed a technique to allow the detection of all interactions between genomic loci in the eukaryotic nucleus followed by deep sequencing. This technology was used to map the organization of the human genome and to examine the spatial proximity of chromosomal loci at one megabase resolution. The map suggests that the genome is partitioned into two spatial compartments that are related to local chromatin state and whose remodeling correlates with changes in the chromatin state.

title: Widespread Shortening of 3′UTRs by Alternative Cleavage and Polyadenylation Activates Oncogenes in Cancer Cells
summary: Cancer cell lines were compared with similarly proliferating non-transformed lines to explain why oncogene proteins can be overexpressed without genetic alteration. Cancer lines often expressed mRNA isoforms with 3' UTRs shortened by alternative cleavage and polyadenylation; these isoforms were more stable and made about ten-fold more protein, partly by escaping microRNA repression. The short IGF2BP1/IMP-1 isoform caused far more oncogenic transformation than the full-length mRNA.
abstract: In cancer cells, genetic alterations can activate proto-oncogenes, thereby contributing to tumorigenesis. However, the protein products of oncogenes are sometimes overexpressed without alteration of the proto-oncogene. Helping to explain this phenomenon, we found that when compared to similarly proliferating nontransformed cell lines, cancer cell lines often expressed substantial amounts of mRNA isoforms with shorter 3' untranslated regions (UTRs). These shorter isoforms usually resulted from alternative cleavage and polyadenylation (APA). The APA had functional consequences, with the shorter mRNA isoforms exhibiting increased stability and typically producing ten-fold more protein, in part through the loss of microRNA-mediated repression. Moreover, expression of the shorter mRNA isoform of the proto-oncogene IGF2BP1/IMP-1 led to far more oncogenic transformation than did expression of the full-length, annotated mRNA. The high incidence of APA in cancer cells, with consequent loss of 3'UTR repressive elements, suggests a pervasive role for APA in oncogene activation without genetic alteration.

title: Potential etiologic and functional implications of genome-wide association loci for human diseases and traits
summary: Introduces an online catalog of published GWAS SNP-trait associations and uses it to describe trait-associated SNPs. These SNPs were common (median risk allele frequency 36%) with modest effects (median OR 1.33). Compared with random array SNPs, they were enriched in nonsynonymous sites (OR 3.9) and 5-kb promoter regions (OR 2.3), were depleted in intergenic regions, and showed little enrichment in regions under positive selection.
abstract: We have developed an online catalog of SNP-trait associations from published genome-wide association studies for use in investigating genomic characteristics of trait/disease-associated SNPs (TASs). Reported TASs were common [median risk allele frequency 36%, interquartile range (IQR) 21%−53%] and were associated with modest effect sizes [median odds ratio (OR) 1.33, IQR 1.20–1.61]. Among 20 genomic annotation sets, reported TASs were significantly overrepresented only in nonsynonymous sites [OR = 3.9 (2.2−7.0), p = 3.5 × 10 −7 ] and 5kb-promoter regions [OR = 2.3 (1.5−3.6), p = 3 × 10 −4 ] compared to SNPs randomly selected from genotyping arrays. Although 88% of TASs were intronic (45%) or intergenic (43%), TASs were not overrepresented in introns and were significantly depleted in intergenic regions [OR = 0.44 (0.34−0.58), p = 2.0 × 10 −9 ]. Only slightly more TASs than expected by chance were predicted to be in regions under positive selection [OR = 1.3 (0.8−2.1), p = 0.2]. This new online resource, together with bioinformatic predictions of the underlying functionality at trait/disease-associated loci, is well-suited to guide future investigations of the role of common variants in complex disease etiology.

title: WGCNA: an R package for weighted correlation network analysis
summary: WGCNA is an R package that brings weighted correlation network methods together in one consistent toolkit, with tutorials. It builds co-expression networks, detects modules of highly correlated genes, summarizes each module by its eigengene or an intramodular hub gene, and relates modules to external sample traits. It also screens genes to find candidate biomarkers or therapeutic targets.
abstract: Background Correlation networks are increasingly being used in bioinformatics applications. For example, weighted gene co-expression network analysis is a systems biology method for describing the correlation patterns among genes across microarray samples. Weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) can be used for finding clusters (modules) of highly correlated genes, for summarizing such clusters using the module eigengene or an intramodular hub gene, for relating modules to one another and to external sample traits (using eigengene network methodology), and for calculating module membership measures. Correlation networks facilitate network based gene screening methods that can be used to identify candidate biomarkers or therapeutic targets. These methods have been successfully applied in various biological contexts, e.g. cancer, mouse genetics, yeast genetics, and analysis of brain imaging data. While parts of the correlation network methodology have been described in separate publications, there is a need to provide a user-friendly, comprehensive, and consistent software implementation and an accompanying tutorial. Results The WGCNA R software package is a comprehensive collection of R functions for performing various aspects of weighted correlation network analysis. The package includes functions for network construction, module detection, gene selection, calculations of topological properties, data simulation, visualization, and interfacing with external software. Along with the R package we also present R software tutorials. While the methods development was motivated by gene expression data, the underlying data mining approach can be applied to a variety of different settings. Conclusion The WGCNA package provides R functions for weighted correlation network analysis, e.g. co-expression network analysis of gene expression data. The R package along with its source code and additional material are freely available at http://www.genetics.ucla.edu/labs/horvath/CoexpressionNetwork/Rpackages/WGCNA.

title: Proliferating Cells Express mRNAs with Shortened 3' Untranslated Regions and Fewer MicroRNA Target Sites
summary: Activated primary mouse CD4+ T cells showed a conserved shift toward upstream polyadenylation sites, producing shorter 3' UTRs, and this shift tracked proliferation across many cell types and tissues. Forcing expression of full-length 3' UTRs lowered protein output, which deleting predicted microRNA target sites sometimes reversed. Proliferation therefore goes with a broad loss of 3' UTR-based regulation.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) stability, localization, and translation are largely determined by sequences in the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR). We found a conserved increase in expression of mRNAs terminating at upstream polyadenylation sites after activation of primary murine CD4 + T lymphocytes. This program, resulting in shorter 3′UTRs, is a characteristic of gene expression during immune cell activation and correlates with proliferation across diverse cell types and tissues. Forced expression of full-length 3′UTRs conferred reduced protein expression. In some cases the reduction in protein expression could be reversed by deletion of predicted microRNA target sites in the variably included region. Our data indicate that gene expression is coordinately regulated, such that states of increased proliferation are associated with widespread reductions in the 3′UTR-based regulatory capacity of mRNAs.

title: SPIKE – a database, visualization and analysis tool of cellular signaling pathways
summary: SPIKE is a community knowledge base for organizing and interpreting cellular signaling pathways. It has three parts: a tiered database holding curated literature interactions alongside data from large public sources, an interactive visualization tool that can overlay genomic and proteomic data on pathway maps, and an inference engine that searches networks for new functional links. Registered users can upload data so that research groups can build the database together.
abstract: Biological signaling pathways that govern cellular physiology form an intricate web of tightly regulated interlocking processes. Data on these regulatory networks are accumulating at an unprecedented pace. The assimilation, visualization and interpretation of these data have become a major challenge in biological research, and once met, will greatly boost our ability to understand cell functioning on a systems level. To cope with this challenge, we are developing the SPIKE knowledge-base of signaling pathways. SPIKE contains three main software components: 1) A database (DB) of biological signaling pathways. Carefully curated information from the literature and data from large public sources constitute distinct tiers of the DB. 2) A visualization package that allows interactive graphic representations of regulatory interactions stored in the DB and superposition of functional genomic and proteomic data on the maps. 3) An algorithmic inference engine that analyzes the networks for novel functional interplays between network components. SPIKE is designed and implemented as a community tool and therefore provides a user-friendly interface that allows registered users to upload data to SPIKE DB. Our vision is that the DB will be populated by a distributed and highly collaborative effort undertaken by multiple groups in the research community, where each group contributes data in its field of expertise. The integrated capabilities of SPIKE make it a powerful platform for the analysis of signaling networks and the integration of knowledge on such networks with omics data.

title: PLINK: A Tool Set for Whole-Genome Association and Population-Based Linkage Analyses
source: The American Journal of Human Genetics
summary: PLINK is an open-source C/C++ toolset for whole-genome association studies that can quickly handle hundreds of thousands of markers in thousands of individuals. It covers data management, summary statistics, population stratification, association testing and identity-by-descent estimation. It focuses on using identity-by-state and identity-by-descent sharing to correct for stratification and to find long shared segments between distant relatives, which could help map loci carrying several rare variants.
abstract: Whole-genome association studies (WGAS) bring new computational, as well as analytic, challenges to researchers. Many existing genetic-analysis tools are not designed to handle such large data sets in a convenient manner and do not necessarily exploit the new opportunities that whole-genome data bring. To address these issues, we developed PLINK, an open-source C/C++ WGAS tool set. With PLINK, large data sets comprising hundreds of thousands of markers genotyped for thousands of individuals can be rapidly manipulated and analyzed in their entirety. As well as providing tools to make the basic analytic steps computationally efficient, PLINK also supports some novel approaches to whole-genome data that take advantage of whole-genome coverage. We introduce PLINK and describe the five main domains of function: data management, summary statistics, population stratification, association analysis, and identity-by-descent estimation. In particular, we focus on the estimation and use of identity-by-state and identity-by-descent information in the context of population-based whole-genome studies. This information can be used to detect and correct for population stratification and to identify extended chromosomal segments that are shared identical by descent between very distantly related individuals. Analysis of the patterns of segmental sharing has the potential to map disease loci that contain multiple rare variants in a population-based linkage analysis.

title: Genome-Wide Mapping of in Vivo Protein-DNA Interactions
summary: ChIP-seq combines chromatin immunoprecipitation with ultrahigh-throughput sequencing to map where transcription factors bind across the whole genome in vivo. Applied to NRSF/REST, it found 1946 binding sites in the human genome with ±50 bp resolution and high accuracy (ROC area ≥0.96). The precise positions revealed noncanonical NRSF motifs and new candidate targets, including key regulators of pancreatic islet development.
abstract: In vivo protein-DNA interactions connect each transcription factor with its direct targets to form a gene network scaffold. To map these protein-DNA interactions comprehensively across entire mammalian genomes, we developed a large-scale chromatin immunoprecipitation assay (ChIPSeq) based on direct ultrahigh-throughput DNA sequencing. This sequence census method was then used to map in vivo binding of the neuron-restrictive silencer factor (NRSF; also known as REST, for repressor element–1 silencing transcription factor) to 1946 locations in the human genome. The data display sharp resolution of binding position [±50 base pairs (bp)], which facilitated our finding motifs and allowed us to identify noncanonical NRSF-binding motifs. These ChIPSeq data also have high sensitivity and specificity [ROC (receiver operator characteristic) area ≥ 0.96] and statistical confidence ( P <10 –4 ), properties that were important for inferring new candidate interactions. These include key transcription factors in the gene network that regulates pancreatic islet cell development.

title: Newborn Hearing Screening — A Silent Revolution
EXPANDER – an integrative program suite for microarray data analysis
summary: EXPANDER 2.0 is an integrated package that lets biologists run the whole microarray analysis workflow in one place. It covers normalization and filtering, clustering and biclustering, Gene Ontology enrichment, and promoter cis-element analysis to find the transcription factors behind expression changes. It comes with precompiled GO and promoter data for yeast, worm, fly, rat, mouse and human.
abstract: Gene expression microarrays are a prominent experimental tool in functional genomics which has opened the opportunity for gaining global, systems-level understanding of transcriptional networks. Experiments that apply this technology typically generate overwhelming volumes of data, unprecedented in biological research. Therefore the task of mining meaningful biological knowledge out of the raw data is a major challenge in bioinformatics. Of special need are integrative packages that provide biologist users with advanced but yet easy to use, set of algorithms, together covering the whole range of steps in microarray data analysis. Here we present the EXPANDER 2.0 (EXPression ANalyzer and DisplayER) software package. EXPANDER 2.0 is an integrative package for the analysis of gene expression data, designed as a 'one-stop shop' tool that implements various data analysis algorithms ranging from the initial steps of normalization and filtering, through clustering and biclustering, to high-level functional enrichment analysis that points to biological processes that are active in the examined conditions, and to promoter cis-regulatory elements analysis that elucidates transcription factors that control the observed transcriptional response. EXPANDER is available with pre-compiled functional Gene Ontology (GO) and promoter sequence-derived data files for yeast, worm, fly, rat, mouse and human, supporting high-level analysis applied to data obtained from these six organisms. EXPANDER integrated capabilities and its built-in support of multiple organisms make it a very powerful tool for analysis of microarray data. The package is freely available for academic users at http://www.cs.tau.ac.il/~rshamir/expander

title: Transcription profiling of inner ears from Pou4f3ddl/ddl identifies Gfi1 as a target of the Pou4f3 deafness gene
summary: To find genes regulated by the hair-cell transcription factor Pou4f3 (mutated in human DFNA15 hearing loss), inner ears of E16.5 wild-type and Pou4f3 mutant mice were compared on high-density oligonucleotide microarrays, with RT-PCR and in situ hybridization used to confirm hits. Gfi1 expression dropped significantly without Pou4f3 and tracked its expression pattern. Gfi1 mutants showed outer hair cell degeneration like Pou4f3 mutants, making Gfi1 the first known downstream target of a hair-cell-specific transcription factor.
abstract: Pou4f3 (Brn3.1, Brn3c) is a class IV POU domain transcription factor that has a central function in the development of all hair cells in the human and mouse inner ear sensory epithelia. A mutation of POU4F3 underlies human autosomal dominant non-syndromic progressive hearing loss DFNA15. Through a comparison of inner ear gene expression profiles of E16.5 wild-type and Pou4f3 mutant deaf mice using a high density oligonucleotide microarray, we identified the gene encoding growth factor independence 1 (Gfi1) as a likely in vivo target gene regulated by Pou4f3. To validate this result, we performed semi-quantitative RT-PCR and in situ hybridizations for Gfi1 on wild-type and Pou4f3 mutant mice. Our results demonstrate that a deficiency of Pou4f3 leads to a statistically significant reduction in Gfi1 expression levels and that the dynamics of Gfi1 mRNA abundance closely follow the pattern of expression for Pou4f3. To examine the role of Gfi1 in the pathogenesis of Pou4f3-related deafness, we performed comparative analyses of the embryonic inner ears of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 mouse mutants using immunohistochemistry and scanning electron microscopy. The loss of Gfi1 results in outer hair cell degeneration, which appears comparable to that observed in Pou4f3 mutants. These results identify Gfi1 as the first downstream target of a hair cell specific transcription factor and suggest that outer hair cell degeneration in Pou4f3 mutants is largely or entirely a result of the loss of expression of Gfi1.

title: Prediction of Mammalian MicroRNA Targets
summary: Which mRNAs do vertebrate miRNAs regulate? Searching for conserved pairing to the miRNA 5′ region predicted more than 400 mammalian target genes. False-positive rates estimated with shuffled controls were 31% for human/mouse/rat targets and 22% when pufferfish was included.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) can play important gene regulatory roles in nematodes, insects, and plants by basepairing to mRNAs to specify posttranscriptional repression of these messages. However, the mRNAs regulated by vertebrate miRNAs are all unknown. Here we predict more than 400 regulatory target genes for the conserved vertebrate miRNAs by identifying mRNAs with conserved pairing to the 5' region of the miRNA and evaluating the number and quality of these complementary sites. Rigorous tests using shuffled miRNA controls supported a majority of these predictions, with the fraction of false positives estimated at 31% for targets identified in human, mouse, and rat and 22% for targets identified in pufferfish as well as mammals. Eleven predicted targets (out of 15 tested) were supported experimentally using a HeLa cell reporter system. The predicted regulatory targets of mammalian miRNAs were enriched for genes involved in transcriptional regulation but also encompassed an unexpectedly broad range of other functions.

title: STRING: a web-server to retrieve and display the repeatedly occurring neighbourhood of a gene
summary: Genes that repeatedly sit next to each other across genomes tend to encode functionally linked proteins. STRING (search tool for recurring instances of neighbouring genes) runs iterative searches to find genes that recur near a query gene and displays them in genomic context, yielding candidate functional partners. As an example, it suggested a functional context for an RNA methylase with unknown specificity.
abstract: The repeated occurrence of genes in each other's neighbourhood on genomes has been shown to indicate a functional association between the proteins they encode. Here we introduce STRING (search tool for recurring instances of neighbouring genes), a tool to retrieve and display the genes a query gene repeatedly occurs with in clusters on the genome. The tool performs iterative searches and visualises the results in their genomic context. By finding the genomically associated genes for a query, it delineates a set of potentially functionally associated genes. The usefulness of STRING is illustrated with an example that suggests a functional context for an RNA methylase with unknown specificity.

title: Connexin 26 mutations in hereditary non-syndromic sensorineural deafness
summary: To find genes behind non-syndromic sensorineural deafness, a pedigree with autosomal dominant deafness and three recessive pedigrees linked to DFNB1 (13q11-12) were studied. A connexin 26 (Cx26, gap junction) mutation segregated with dominant profound deafness, and premature stop codons in Cx26 were found in the recessive families. Cx26 is highly expressed in human cochlea, making it the first known non-syndromic autosomal deafness gene.
abstract: Severe deafness or hearing impairment is the most prevalent inherited sensory disorder, affecting about 1 in 1,000 children. Most deafness results from peripheral auditory defects that occur as a consequence of either conductive (outer or middle ear) or sensorineuronal (cochlea) abnormalities. Although a number of mutant genes have been identified that are responsible for syndromic (multiple phenotypic disease) deafness such as Waardenburg syndrome and Usher 1B syndrome, little is known about the genetic basis of non-syndromic (single phenotypic disease) deafness. Here we study a pedigree containing cases of autosomal dominant deafness and have identified a mutation in the gene encoding the gap-junction protein connexin 26 (Cx26) that segregates with the profound deafness in the family. Cx26 mutations resulting in premature stop codons were also found in three autosomal recessive non-syndromic sensorineuronal deafness pedigrees, genetically linked to chromosome 13q11-12 (DFNB1), where the Cx26 gene is localized. Immunohistochemical staining of human cochlear cells for Cx26 demonstrated high levels of expression. To our knowledge, this is the first non-syndromic sensorineural autosomal deafness susceptibility gene to be identified, which implicates Cx26 as an important component of the human cochlea.

title: Gene Burden Testing for Rare and Genetic Disease Studies: A Practical Beginner-Oriented Workflow
summary: This methods chapter gives a beginner-oriented, disease-agnostic workflow for gene burden testing of rare variants in sequencing studies. It covers study design, QC, annotation, qualifying-variant definitions, choosing burden versus kernel tests, covariates and interpretation, with emphasis on reproducibility choices such as ancestry matching and frequency thresholds.
abstract: Gene burden testing is a practical analytic framework for evaluating whether multiple rare variants within a gene, transcript, or biologically defined variant set are collectively associated with disease. This strategy is especially useful in rare disease and sequencing-based genetic studies because most individual rare variants are too uncommon to achieve adequate statistical power on their own, whereas aggregating them into a biologically meaningful set can increase the ability to detect association. This chapter is written as a general bioinformatics method rather than as a disease-specific protocol, so that it can be applied to Mendelian disorders, complex diseases enriched for rare coding alleles, unresolved exome cases, and candidate genes prioritized from wet-lab experiments. The workflow covers study design, data preparation, sample and variant quality control, variant annotation, definition of qualifying variants, selection of burden and kernel-based tests, covariate adjustment, and interpretation of positive and negative findings. Emphasis is placed on methods that are accessible to graduate students and physician-scientists using public or institutional sequencing datasets, and on practical decisions that strongly influence reproducibility, such as ancestry matching, allele-frequency thresholds, phenotype handling, and sensitivity analyses. The chapter also positions gene burden testing within the broader landscape of modern statistical genetics, including collapsing methods, weighted burden tests, variance-component methods, and extensions toward oligogenic or digenic disease architectures.

title: A Graded Immune-Cell-Resolved cis-eQTL Mendelian Randomisation Screen Across Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Related Immune Phenotypes
summary: The authors audited cis-eQTL instruments for 15 sorted immune-cell types from DICE and used them in Mendelian randomisation against SLE and seven related FinnGen outcomes, adding colocalisation and genomic-control sensitivity analyses. After outcome-specific FDR control, 424 gene-outcome relationships remained. The SLE signals were concentrated in the MHC, and most non-MHC hits were for rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune hypothyroidism; the authors present this as a hypothesis-generating screen.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a genetically complex autoimmune disease. Whole-blood expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analyses capture average regulatory effects across leukocytes, whereas SLE involves immune processes that depend on cell context. Therefore, a cell-resolved screen requires rigorous verification of instrument identity, allele orientation, and the multiple-testing denominator before biological interpretation. AIMS: To conduct an identity-first, immune-cell-resolved cis-eQTL Mendelian randomization (MR) screen across SLE and related immune phenotypes and distinguish statistical signal counts from variant-level, regional, and cross-cell evidence. STUDY DESIGN: Two-sample summary-data cis-eQTL MR and secondary evidence synthesis using 15 primary human immune-cell types from Database of Immune-Cell Expression (DICE) and eight disease outcomes from FinnGen release 12. METHODS: All 19,009 gene-cell-type instruments were audited before outcome testing. Only 6,525 instruments with exact variant identities and concordant DICE effect information were retained for analysis. Wald ratios were calculated for 48,958 outcome-instrument tests, with the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure applied separately to each outcome to control the false discovery rate (FDR). Both prespecified infection-negative controls were then matched exactly by cell type, gene, and rsID, with each contributing 6,119 tests. For the sensitivity analysis, each chi-square statistic was divided by its outcome-specific genomic control inflation factor (lambda GC), and the BH procedure was reapplied within each outcome. Audited signals were summarized by unique single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), linkage disequilibrium (LD)-independent index signal, gene-outcome relationship, and MHC location. Regional colocalization, bounded multivariable MR, and Gene Ontology analyses provided additional layers of evidence. RESULTS: The identity-first audit retained 6,525 of 19,009 instruments. Of these, 6,122 matched at least one outcome, whereas 403 did not. Among the 48,958 strict tests, 1,186 rows reached an outcome-specific FDR of less than 0.05, corresponding to 304 genes, 494 SNPs, 868 cell-gene pairs, and 424 gene-outcome relationships. LD auditing resolved 670 outcome-specific lead-SNP records into 639 reference-matched records and 31 separately reported records, yielding 288 LD-independent index signals. The primary SLE analysis identified 55 FDR-significant signals, 23 genes, 29 SNPs, and 11 index signals; 16 of the 23 genes and 6 of the 11 index signals were located in the MHC. The second SLE definition showed a similarly strong concentration of signals in the MHC. Most non-MHC disease signals were associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and autoimmune hypothyroidism (AIH). Lambda GC ranged from 1.17 to 2.03 across disease outcomes. Following outcome-specific lambda adjustment, 483 disease rows remained FDR-significant. The greatest reductions in significant rows occurred for AIH (691-211), RA (213-103), and strict MI (83-11). The negative controls, other sepsis and bacterial infection not otherwise specified (NOS), each matched 6,119 tests and had lambda GC values of 1.06 and 1.08, respectively. No FDR-significant rows were identified for bacterial infection NOS. CONCLUSION: This revised analysis provides a graded and auditable screening framework rather than a definitive list of SLE risk genes. The primary SLE evidence is concentrated in the 6p21/MHC region, whereas broader non-MHC candidate signals arise predominantly from related immune phenotypes. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require independent replication and experimental validation.

title: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
summary: Adjusting rare-variant tests for a polygenic risk score helps with quantitative traits but gives little or no power gain for binary traits. The authors developed the liability threshold burden test (LTBT), which models rare-variant burden and PRS together under a liability threshold model, and showed in simulations that it controls false positives and is more sensitive than existing methods. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis sequencing data, it found and replicated a new association between rare predicted-damaging missense variants in HTRA3 and IPF.
abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individual's genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

title: Aging out of the blue: Region-specific epigenetic clock calibration for a blue zone with the DNAm SuperLearner
summary: Trained a SuperLearner ensemble of existing epigenetic clocks and machine learners on 875 non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans (CRELES) and used it for a calibrated test of age acceleration in 206 residents of the Nicoya blue zone. Uncalibrated clocks gave conflicting answers (from ~3 years younger to ~4 years older). After age-stratified calibration, only a small advantage of about 0.35 years remained, mostly in the oldest participants.
abstract: Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at CpG sites, providing robust predictions of mortality and morbidity risk. "Blue zones," regions of exceptional longevity, offer a unique opportunity to investigate how biological aging diverges from chronological age. However, standard clocks are typically trained on large, heterogeneous datasets, reflecting average population trends rather than region-specific dynamics. Using data from the Costa Rican Longevity and Healthy Aging Study (CRELES), we profiled DNA methylation from residents of the Nicoya blue zone (n = 206) and a reference population in other parts of Costa Rica (n = 875). We propose training a SuperLearner, an ensemble machine learning approach, on the non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans to optimize predictive performance across existing clocks and flexible machine learners. By its Oracle property, the SuperLearner's weighted combination of algorithms performs asymptotically as well as the best possible combination of the candidate predictors. We then used this trained model to construct a calibrated hypothesis test comparing Epigenetic Age Acceleration (EAA) distributions between the blue zone region and the reference population. Before calibration or covariate adjustment, estimates for Nicoyans depended heavily on the chosen clock. The SuperLearner placed them about three years younger on average (R̄1=-3.05, 95% CI [-3.64,-2.46]), whereas DNAmFitAge placed them almost four years older (R̄1=3.59, 95% CI [3.02,4.17]). Mean calibration to non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans made estimates consistent across clocks, with an estimated EAA advantage to approximately two years (Δ̂=-1.96, 95% CI [-2.56,-1.37]). After age-stratified calibration within 10-year age groups, only a small EAA advantage (Δ̂=-0.35, 95% CI [-0.64,-0.05]) remained, concentrated among the oldest participants. This approach provides a robust and reproducible framework for estimating longevity in distinct regions when a relevant reference population is available.

title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts regulatory activity and variant effects across cell states
summary: Single-cell atlases rarely have enough donors for direct eQTL mapping, so the authors built AlphaGenome 2, a sequence model conditioned on a tissue, cell type or cell state and trained on human and mouse single-cell atlases plus bulk data. It doubles recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision compared with fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialised models, and it generalises to unseen datasets without fine-tuning. The authors also release enhancer-gene links and variant scores for 7 million common variants across hundreds of cell types.
abstract: Most genetic variants associated with human traits and diseases lie in non-coding DNA, where they can alter gene regulation in specific cell types and states. Single-cell atlases chart these states across tissues and development, but rarely profile enough donors to associate variants with expression directly. Deep learning models could bridge this gap by predicting variant effects from DNA sequence, yet they poorly distinguish related cell states and require fine-tuning for new datasets. Here we present AlphaGenome 2 (AG2), which substantially advances cell-type-specific prediction of regulatory activity and variant effects for gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Trained on organism-wide human and mouse single-cell atlases and bulk functional genomics data, AG2 takes as input a 1-Mb DNA sequence and a condition specifying a target tissue, cell type, or cell state. Conditioning enables AG2 to impute unmeasured epigenomic tracks and predict multimodal variant effects across cell types. Inferring this condition directly from gene expression extends AG2 to unseen datasets and cell states without fine-tuning. AG2 outperforms fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 and specialized models trained on target datasets, doubling recall of causal single-cell eQTLs at 90% precision. AG2 also achieves state-of-the-art enhancer-gene linking and can pinpoint causal variants at complex trait loci. Across hundreds of human cell types, we generated an atlas of enhancer-gene links and scores for 7 million common variants. As single-cell profiling expands across development, tissues, and disease cohorts, AG2 provides a blueprint for turning observational atlases into variant effect maps.

title: Both Endogenous Enhancer and Retrotransposon Inserted Nearby Are Required to Induce Ectopic Expression in Danforth's Short Tail Mutation
summary: Investigates why the endogenous retrovirus insertion in Danforth's short tail mice drives ectopic Ptf1a expression in the notochord. Mutating the Ptf1a auto-regulatory enhancer or the ERV showed that both are needed for the vertebral phenotype, with the core activity in the enhancer half closest to the ERV. The PTF1 complex itself was not required.
abstract: Danforth's short tail (Sd) is a semi-dominant mutation that causes vertebral column defects. In Sd mice, an endogenous retrovirus (ERV) is inserted upstream of the pancreatic transcription factor 1A (Ptf1a) gene, and the ectopic expression of Ptf1a in the notochord causes the Sd phenotype. However, the mechanisms underlying ectopic expression remain unclear. We focused on the Ptf1a enhancer, known as the Auto-Regulatory Enhancer (ARE), near the ERV insertion site. We introduced various mutations into the ARE and ERV on the Sd genome. Both the ARE-deleted-ERV-retained Sd mice and ARE-retained-ERV-deleted Sd mice lost their vertebral column defects, which indicates the importance of the coexistence of ARE and ERV. Among two CpG islands and two PTF1 boxes in the ARE, the proximal half region close to the ERV was identified as the core element responsible for ectopic expression. Although PTF1 boxes are known binding sites for the PTF1 complex containing Ptf1a, the detection of ectopic expression even in Ptf1a-deficient Sd mice indicated that the PTF1 complex is not required for ectopic expression. These results indicate that ARE and the inserted ERV act in concert to induce ectopic expression and provide a new example of the mutagenic mechanism of ERV.

title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence
summary: CellColocDB is a database of systematic GWAS-QTL colocalization meant to link disease loci to genes and the cellular contexts they act in. It runs coloc.abf across 2805 GWAS (1201 traits) and 316 bulk, sorted-cell and single-cell QTL contexts, adds coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI evidence, and links the top SNPs to fine-mapping results in CAUSALdb2. The release holds about 1.6 million colocalizations with PP.H4 of at least 0.8, which can be searched by disease, gene, locus or QTL context.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified disease-associated loci, but linking these signals to molecular mechanisms remains difficult because of linkage disequilibrium and context-dependent genetic regulation. CellColocDB is a disease- and window-centred resource integrating GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell, and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release includes 2805 GWAS datasets covering 1201 diseases and traits and 40 516 GWAS windows, together with 23 QTL sources, 316 QTL contexts, and 89 842 molecular features. CellColocDB contains 3 572 118 coloc.abf results with PP.H4 > 0.5, including 1 609 418 with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8. Analyses are organized as GWAS dataset × GWAS window × QTL context × molecular feature tasks, allowing contexts and molecular features to be compared within the same GWAS region. coloc.abf is the primary colocalization analysis, with coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI providing complementary evidence where available. Task-specific ABF top SNPs are linked to CAUSALdb2 fine-mapping results from seven methods. Results are available through disease-, QTL context-, gene-, and locus-level views, with regional association tracks and matched variants, and can be queried by gene, genomic region, or GWAS window ID. CellColocDB is freely available at http://www.mulinlab.org/colocdb/.

title: DGIdb in 2026: an interoperable resource for the druggable genome
summary: This update of the Drug-Gene Interaction Database adds three new interaction sources, including the PRISM Repurposing Dataset and the Broad Drug Repurposing Hub. For reproducible programmatic use it adds Python/R clients (dgiPy, dgiR), versioned Docker images and a public archive of current and past releases, which widens FAIR access to drug-gene data for drug-repurposing workflows.
abstract: The Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb; https://dgidb.org) is an open-access aggregate knowledgebase that normalizes and centralizes drug-gene interaction and gene annotation data from diverse therapeutic and biomedical sources. Since its previous update, DGIdb has expanded its data content and added new tooling to better support programmatic access and local deployment. This release updates existing sources and incorporates three new sources of interaction data, including annotation data from the Molecular Oncology Almanac, the PRISM Repurposing Dataset, and the Broad Institute Drug Repurposing Hub. To streamline data access for computational workflows, we have developed dgiPy and dgiR, Python and R client libraries that provide standardized access to the DGIdb API. We additionally now provide versioned Docker images and a public data repository containing current and historical DGIdb data releases in TSV and SQL formats. Together with continued improvements to the web interface, these new resources expand FAIR, transparent, and reproducible access to drug-gene interaction data in the bioinformatics community.

title: DIANA-miTED v2: an expanded microRNA tissue expression database with an integrated healthy-tissue reference atlas
summary: The update grows the uniformly processed human small RNA-seq collection from about 15,000 to nearly 50,000 profiles, adding GTEx v10 samples and many more from SRA, and it now covers 2,656 mature miRNAs across 96 tissues, 437 cell lines and 503 diseases. It provides a healthy-tissue reference atlas (more than 23,000 healthy donors), keeping tumour-adjacent normal samples separate. It also adds a body-map interface, co-expression networks, downloads and a REST API.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression that exhibit tissue- and condition-associated expression patterns. Interpreting their abundance in disease or experimental contexts requires a physiological reference. DIANA-miTED v2 expands its uniformly processed and manually curated collection from 15 183 to 49 630 human small RNA-sequencing profiles spanning healthy tissues, cell lines, and disease states. To our knowledge, this is the largest such collection of human miRNA expression profiles assembled to date. It adds 16 746 Genotype-Tissue Expression V10 profiles and expands the Sequence Read Archive collection from 4142 to 21 843, alongside the existing The Cancer Genome Atlas collection. Expression is quantified for 2656 mature miRNAs, with harmonized metadata covering 96 tissues or organs, 437 cell lines, and 503 diseases. Healthy-donor coverage increases from 709 to 23 281, with 1471 tumour-adjacent-normal profiles classified separately. The database distinguishes primary tissues and biofluids from cultured and derived preparations. A redesigned tissue-centric interface provides a body-map picker, sublocation refinement, multi-miRNA and multi-tissue querying, cohort summaries, and descriptive longitudinal browsing. Co-expression capabilities include pairwise Spearman correlation and precomputed WGCNA modules, with 263 overview and 105 source/project-specific reference networks. Quantified counts, reads per million values, metadata, and query results are available through downloads and a REST API. DIANA-miTED v2 is freely available, without registration, at http://microrna.gr/mitedv2.

title: Enduring DNA Methylation Marks of Blast and Trauma Exposures in Warfighters
summary: Ran EWAS of career blast and trauma exposure in 220 military breachers and grenade operators, built methylation risk scores for these exposures, and tested DunedinPACE age acceleration. The scores reached external AUCs of about 0.72-0.74 (0.52 for blast in grenade operators), and the trauma score was linked to slower reaction time after blast exposure. Exposures were also associated with faster DunedinPACE.
abstract: Introduction: Service members (SMs) in high-risk military occupational specialties can sustain hundreds to thousands of career blast and psychological trauma exposures, yet objective biomarkers capturing effects of these exposures remain elusive. DNA methylation offers a stable signature of environmental exposures and mechanisms underlying long-term neurological and psychiatric sequelae. The study objective was to identify DNA methylation signatures of military service and combat exposures in SMs and evaluate whether methylation risk scores (MRS) predict chronic exposures and neurocognitive performance among SMs exposed to blast overpressure before and after military tactical training operations. Materials and methods: This was a retrospective cohort epigenome-wide association study of 190 breachers and 30 hand grenade operators (all male) enrolled during US military training operations. Data included demographics, medical and combat exposure history, and blood samples collected during training.
