Neurocognitive performance was evaluated pre- and post-training in breachers using the Defense Automated Neurobehavioral Assessment (DANA). Combat factors (CF1-blast and CF2-trauma) derived by exploratory factor analysis; association of combat factors with epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) measured by DunedinPACE epigenetic clock; epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) of combat factors; MRS models capturing career blast and trauma exposures; and associations between MRS and neurocognitive performance on DANA pre- and post-training. Results: EAA significantly correlated with military service duration, CF1-blast, and CF2-trauma (all P < .01). EWAS identified 12 genomic regions associated with CF1-blast and 22 with CF2-trauma, including genes implicated in neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier integrity, and auditory functioning. MRS models achieved internal validation AUC of 88% and 86% for CF1-blast and CF2-trauma, respectively. External validation yielded AUC of 74% for both MRS models in breachers, and 52% and 72% in grenade operators. CF2-trauma MRS was significantly associated with increased procedural reaction time on DANA subtask following blast exposure (β = 21.98, P = .002), independent of blast magnitude and service duration. Conclusions: DNA methylation signatures of career blast and trauma exposures were associated with epigenetic age acceleration and diminished neurocognitive performance in SMs engaged in tactical operations, supporting the utility of epigenetic biomarkers for objective exposure assessment and operational readiness.

title: GI-DB: a comprehensive variant database for exploring the extensive genetic diversity of the Indian population
summary: South Asians are underrepresented in global variant resources, so the GenomeIndia initiative sequenced about 10,000 genomes from 83 Indian populations. GI-DB is the public browser for this data: it catalogs 136 million high-confidence variants, 44 million of them missing from other global and South Asian databases. It gives allele frequencies by tribal versus non-tribal group, region and language family, with annotations and comparisons to 1000 Genomes, gnomAD and GenomeAsia.
abstract: The Indian population, characterized by extensive ethnolinguistic and biogeographical diversity, is significantly underrepresented in global genomic resources limiting the development of genomic medicine in South Asia. To address this, ~10 000 genomes from 83 populations were sequenced as part of the GenomeIndia initiative (Department of Biotechnology, Government of India). Here, we present GI-DB (accessible at https://ibdc.dbt.gov.in/gidb/), a public resource cataloging 136 million high-confidence variants, including 44 million variants which are not present in other global and South Asian databases. GI-DB serves as a population-specific reference resource for genetic variation across Indian populations. It can support the interpretation of clinically relevant variations for rare disease, complex disorders, and pharmacogenomics. The database is structured to provide allele frequency stratification across tribal and non-tribal groups, biogeography, and ethnolinguistic categories. The interactive browser facilitates exploration of variants and genes of interest, offering detailed annotations from tools like VEP, ClinVar, and comparisons with global databases like 1000 Genomes, gnomAD, and GenomeAsia. Researchers can search using different modalities and access data programmatically. GI-DB is a foundational resource for genomics-informed public health and clinical genetics, tailored for the Indian population.

title: GausSKAT: A Data-Adaptive Weighted Gaussian Kernel Procedure for Rare-Variant Association Testing Within the SKAT Framework
summary: SKAT almost always uses a weighted-linear kernel, and how well a Gaussian kernel works depends on a bandwidth that cannot be chosen in advance. GausSKAT runs weighted Gaussian SKAT over a data-driven, phenotype-independent grid of bandwidths and combines the resulting p-values with ACAT. In simulations it generally had more power than weighted-linear and IBS SKAT; in Dallas Heart Study triglyceride data its advantage over linear SKAT varied across ANGPTL gene sets.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies have limited power to detect rare-variant associations. The sequence kernel association test (SKAT) enhances power by jointly testing variants within a region, but its power depends on how the kernel represents genetic similarity. The weighted-linear kernel predominates in rare-variant testing, whereas the weighted Gaussian kernel remains less widely used. Varying the Gaussian bandwidth hyperparameter changes the representation of genetic similarity from localized and nonlinear to increasingly linear-like. However, very small hyperparameter values can cause similarities between nonidentical weighted genotype profiles to collapse toward zero, whereas very large values cause the weighted Gaussian kernel to behave increasingly like weighted-linear SKAT and therefore provide little distinct information. Because the underlying genetic architecture is unknown, no single hyperparameter value can be expected to work best across regions. We propose GausSKAT, which evaluates weighted Gaussian SKAT over a phenotype-independent, data-adaptive hyperparameter grid and combines the resulting dependent p values using the aggregated Cauchy association test (ACAT). The grid endpoints are informed by weighted genetic distances and the large-hyperparameter behavior of the covariate-adjusted kernel. In simulations, GausSKAT generally achieved higher power than weighted-linear and weighted identity-by-state SKAT under the genetic architectures considered. The best-performing hyperparameter value varied across settings, supporting aggregation across multiple values. In the Dallas Heart Study analysis of triglyceride levels, the relative performance of GausSKAT and weighted-linear SKAT varied among ANGPTL gene-family variant sets. These findings support GausSKAT as a complementary extension that broadens the similarity structures represented within SKAT.

title: Genetic Dissection of the Mouse Class I Odorant Receptor Gene Cluster
summary: Uses large targeted deletions in the mouse Class I odorant receptor cluster to look for regulatory elements beyond the J element. Removing the centromeric half, which contains J, reduced expression of telomeric genes, while removing the telomeric half increased expression of centromeric genes. This supports J as the main long-range enhancer, with weaker secondary enhancers elsewhere in the cluster.
abstract: Mouse Class I odorant receptor (OR) genes form a single large cluster on chromosome 7, whose expression is regulated by a long-range enhancer known as the J element. Previous studies have shown that a subset of Class I OR genes remains expressed in the absence of the J element, suggesting the presence of additional regulatory elements. However, such elements have not yet been identified. To gain insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying Class I OR gene expression, we performed targeted deletion analyses of the Class I OR gene cluster, using the evolutionarily conserved β-globin genes located near the center of the cluster as a landmark. Deletion of the centromeric region, including the J element, resulted in reduced expression of telomeric Class I OR genes, with a pattern similar to that observed in the J element deletion. In contrast, deletion of the telomeric portion increased the expression of centromeric Class I OR genes. Together with previous findings, these results indicate that the J element functions as the primary enhancer for Class I OR gene expression and suggest the existence of secondary Class I enhancers with weaker activities outside the centromeric region of the cluster.

title: Integrating genetic and lung tissue proteomics data to identify susceptibility proteins for lung cancer
source: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
summary: The authors built genetic models of protein abundance from proteomes of 200 normal lung tissues and applied them in a proteome-wide association study of about 55,000 lung cancer cases. They found 29 risk-associated proteins, 15 of them more than 2 Mb from known GWAS loci, and backed them up with replication, colocalization and SMR. DSP, IL18 and TYMP had the strongest evidence and are targets of approved or late-stage drugs.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Proteins directly impact disease development and act as drug targets. We integrated genetic and lung tissue proteomic data to identify lung cancer susceptibility proteins and evaluated them as candidate drug targets. METHOD: We profiled the proteome and genome in 200 non-neoplastic lung tissue samples and constructed genetic models to predict protein abundance. These models were applied to genome-wide association study (GWAS) data of 55,174 lung cancer cases and 1,294,174 controls to evaluate associations between predicted abundance and lung cancer risk overall and by major histological subtypes. Independent lung tissue proteomic data was used for cross-dataset evaluation, followed by colocalization and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization. Prioritized proteins were cross-referenced against drug databases. RESULTS: We identified 29 lung cancer risk-associated proteins at a false discovery rate 2Mb away from known GWAS risk loci. Among the remaining 14 proteins at known risk loci, five (EPHX2, CLDN18, PSMD5, ARHGAP27, and CYP2S1) showed associations independent of proximal lead variant. Of the 29 proteins, eight were predicted and six were significant in independent data. DSP, IL18 and TYMP proteins demonstrated both reproducible and potential causal evidence and are targeted by six drugs that are FDA-approved or in phase III trials. CONCLUSION: Our study identified novel lung cancer susceptibility proteins and potential therapeutic targets, offering insights into lung cancer biology and informing future translational research.

title: LACA: a cross-species single-cell resource for exploring longevity and aging-associated cellular and molecular programs
summary: The Longevity & Aging Cell Atlas brings together single-cell transcriptomic data from 134 species (over 148 million cells, 190 annotated cell types) and links them to each species' maximum lifespan. It provides tools that correlate genes and cell types with lifespan, plus a centenarian single-cell atlas and a human immune-aging multi-omics atlas. A knowledge graph and a retrieval-augmented assistant help with interpretation.
abstract: Different species can have various maximum lifespans, some with exceptional longevity, yet the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Despite rapid advances in single-cell transcriptomics, resources that systematically connect single-cell gene expression profiles to species lifespan are limited. We hereby present the Longevity & Aging Cell Atlas (LACA), a database that integrates single-cell transcriptomic datasets across 134 species with their maximum lifespans. LACA includes over 148 million cells with 190 annotated cell types from single-cell datasets. LACA also has a cross-species analytical toolbox of longevity gene comparison, gene-lifespan correlation, and cell-lifespan correlation. These tools allow researchers to better interpret both evolutionarily conserved longevity mechanisms and the evolution of species-specific adaptations in longevity mechanisms without extensive computational expertise. LACA also provides a centenarian single-cell atlas and a human immune aging multi-omics atlas, demonstrating the analytical capability of the resource, as well as 11 different modules for longevity-related analysis, an integrated knowledge graph including curated longevity knowledge bases, and a retrieval-augmented research agent to further facilitate functional interpretation. The database is freely available at https://www.longevityaging.net/ or http://8.142.154.29/LACA/.

title: MGnify analyses in 2027: enhancing the depth and breadth of analyses across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenomes, and assembled datasets
summary: MGnify v6 updates EMBL-EBI's standardized microbiome analysis pipelines with amplicon sequence variants, viral and mobilome annotation of assemblies, and a minimal raw-reads analysis. The pipelines were ported to Nextflow with Prefect orchestration for better reuse. New bulk and programmatic access services support large-scale computational use of the data.
abstract: Microbiome derived nucleic acid sequence analysis has become an increasingly important aspect of many scientific fields. MGnify (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics/) provides standardized, versioned analysis pipelines for the taxonomic and functional characterization of microbiome samples. The latest release of the MGnify pipelines (version 6) provides amplicon sequence variant analysis, expanded functional annotations including viral and mobilome for assembly analysis, and a streamlined minimal raw-reads analysis. We have improved the reusability of the pipelines through transition to Nextflow as a workflow language and have undertaken a substantial overhaul of our automation systems, using Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline execution. Finally, we have released a new version of our programmatic and bulk access services to better support large-scale computational access of data, as well as rationalizing our contig browser to improve in-browser performance. These improvements serve to support the use of MGnify pipelines and data products going forward, and improve the AI-readiness of our outputs.

title: MIsoTEx: a mammalian transcript-isoform classification framework and database for exploring tissue distribution, expression stability, and abundance patterns
summary: The authors built a tissue-expression reference at the level of transcript isoforms rather than genes. Using normal adult RNA-seq from GTEx, ARCHS4 and curated SRA datasets, they sorted about 147,000 protein-coding isoforms from human, mouse and rat into ubiquitous and tissue-associated expression classes with relative-abundance subclasses and confidence scores. The database can be queried by gene, transcript, tissue pattern or ortholog, and part of the classification held up against independent RNA-seq and RT-PCR data.
abstract: Alternative splicing generates transcript isoforms with distinct tissue-expression patterns, but resources integrating transcript distribution, abundance consistency, and relative abundance remain limited. We developed MIsoTEx (Mammalian Isoform Tissue Expression Resource), a database and expression-pattern-based classification framework for protein-coding iso-mRNAs in human, mouse, and rat. RNA-seq datasets from GTEx, ARCHS4, and newly curated datasets from SRA were used to construct catalogs, following stringent selection of normal adult tissue samples. Ubiquitously detected iso-mRNAs were classified as uniformly abundant (UUni) or variably abundant (UVar), while tissue-associated iso-mRNAs were classified as tissue-predominant (TPred), tissue-exclusive (TExcl), tissue-poor (TPoor), or tissue-absent (TAbsn). These classes were further divided into five relative-abundance sub-classes, with confidence scores assigned to tissue-associated classifications. MIsoTEx contains ~147 000 protein-coding iso-mRNAs and supports gene- and transcript-based queries, tissue-pattern searches, cross-species comparison of orthologs with concordant expression, and analysis of user-supplied expression data to identify candidate control iso-mRNAs. Comparisons with independent RNA-seq, RT-PCR, and published expression datasets provided support for aspects of the classification framework. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct biological associations among selected expression-based categories. MIsoTEx facilitates transcript-level exploration of mammalian tissue-expression patterns and helps identify candidate reference iso-mRNAs for experimental evaluation. The database can be accessed using the link: https://resources.ibab.ac.in/MIsoTEx/.

title: MatriSpace: Identification and visualization of spatially resolved ECM gene expression patterns in health and disease
summary: MatriSpace is a framework for mining spatial transcriptomics data for extracellular-matrix (matrisome) gene expression. It maps ECM genes to cell populations, tissue niches and functional ECM units. It is available as an R package and a no-code Shiny web app, where users can upload their own data or explore a collection of public datasets.
abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a highly dynamic network of proteins forming the structural organizer of all tissues. Different cell populations contribute to the assembly of the 150+ proteins of a functional ECM. In addition, different ECM subtypes, supporting distinct cellular functions, are found in every organ. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides a unique, yet untapped, opportunity to identify which cell populations contribute to ECM production with spatial context. Applied to healthy and diseased samples, this method can identify ECM changes that could be exploited for therapeutic purposes. Here, we introduce MatriSpace, a computational framework to mine ST datasets with a focus on ECM genes. MatriSpace offers two operating modes: researchers can either upload their own ST datasets or explore a large collection of public datasets. Upon analysis, MatriSpace returns spatially resolved maps of matrisome gene expression in relation to cell populations, at multiple levels: from single-gene analysis to tissue niches and functional ECM units. MatriSpace is available as an R package and an online Shiny App (https://izzilab-matrispace.share.connect.posit.cloud), making it accessible to all users regardless of their level of expertise.

title: OMIGAT: Multi-Feature Enhanced Collaborative Attention and Graph Convolution Model for Cancer Driver Gene Identification
summary: The authors built OMIGAT to rank cancer driver genes despite noisy multi-omics data and incomplete prior interaction networks. It joins genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features with network topology. A global branch learns a feature-similarity graph, a local graph-convolution branch learns from the biological network, and the two are fused adaptively; the model reaches an AUC of 87.46% on the PPNet dataset.
abstract: Human cancers encompass a diverse spectrum of malignancies characterized by extensive molecular diversity, heterogeneous biological behaviors, and distinct evolutionary trajectories. The identification and characterization of cancer driver genes (CDGs) constitute a critical step toward advancing precision oncology and individualized treatment. However, noise interference in multi-omics data, the incompleteness of prior biological networks, and complex topological structures constrain the predictive performance of existing deep learning models. To address these challenges, this study proposes OMIGAT-Omics Multi-modal Integration via Collaborative Attention Transformer and Graph Convolution-a global-local collaborative modeling framework designed for multi-omics noise and complex biological network topology. Specifically, OMIGAT first integrates genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data through a topology-aware multi-omics representation enhancement module and incorporates label-independent topological priors to improve the robustness of gene representations against multi-omics noise while strengthening the representation of hub genes and local functional modules. The model then employs a dual-path learning architecture that operates in parallel at global and local scales. The global representation learner constructs a feature-similarity graph from the enhanced multi-omics representations to capture macro-level long-range functional associations that may be absent from prior biological networks. In contrast, the local structure encoder characterizes micro-level neighborhood topological patterns and functionally related modular structures under biological network constraints, thereby reducing the impact of noisy edges on information propagation. Macro-level functional associations and micro-level neighborhood topology provide complementary discriminative information, which is dynamically integrated through an adaptive fusion mechanism to balance the contributions of global functional similarity and local network structure to CDG prediction. Experimental results show that OMIGAT achieves an AUC of 87.46% on the PPNet dataset, demonstrating strong predictive performance in identifying known CDGs.

title: Overview of recruitment strategies to reach the million milestone and characterization of the Million Veteran Program cohort
summary: Describes how the VA Million Veteran Program used a 2022-2023 multi-channel campaign (calls, mail, email, digital ads) to enroll its millionth participant, and how well each channel worked. The campaign contacted over 6.5 million Veterans and enrolled about 110,000; calls had the highest enrollment rate, while email brought in the most people. It also profiles the full cohort of about 1.02 million mostly male participants, which looks much like the wider VA patient population and is linked to health records for genetic research.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Million Veteran Program (MVP) began in 2011 with the goal of recruiting at least one million Veterans to participate in a large population genetic and health research program. The Million Milestone Campaign (MMC) was implemented between 2022 and 2023 to reach pre-pandemic recruitment rates and the millionth enrollee by Veterans Day of 2023. The objectives are to describe and evaluate the enrollment yield of MMC recruitment strategies and to characterize the cumulative MVP cohort. METHODS: During the MMC, multiple recruitment strategies, including paper invitation mailings, recruitment calls, mass emails, enroll by mail invitations, and digital marketing, were implemented using a "surround sound" model. Strategy effectiveness was assessed for each enrollment modality from September 2022 through July 2024. Email and digital media reach were measured by click-through rates and ads viewed. Standard mean differences were used to compare the demographics of enrollees during the MMC with those of enrollees prior, and the cumulative MVP cohort with those of non-MVP VA users. RESULTS: More than 6.5 million Veterans were contacted and 109,912 enrolled during the MMC. Enrollment rates from recruitment calls (13.7%) were highest, followed by invitations to enroll by mail (7.8%), email (0.8%), and paper invitations (0.6%). Emails yielded the most enrollments (n = 46,999, 43% of total enrollments), followed by recruitment calls (n = 22,069, 20%), paper invitations (n = 16,062, 14.6%), and invitations to enroll by mail (n = 7,762,7.1%). There were small differences in demographics between those enrolled during the MMC and prior enrollees (n = 906,672); likewise, the cumulative cohort (N = 1,016,584) of largely male participants resembles the non-MVP VA user population. CONCLUSIONS: In the year leading to the culmination of one million MVP participants, the multi-strategy MMC resulted in recruiting nearly 110,000 Veterans and informing ongoing recruitment. Combined strategies used in a surround sound model of recruitment yielded enrollments aligned with pre-pandemic rates and accumulated one-tenth the largest cohort of Veterans in VA research history. MVP's integration within the VHA as a learning health care system, along with linkages to health records and other data sources, is a resource for investigators to improve Veteran health care with precision medicine.

title: Polygenic risk scores for sleep: from portability to clinical utility
summary: Single-author perspective on polygenic risk scores for sleep traits and disorders, covering how well they transfer across populations and whether they are clinically useful. No abstract is available, so this summary is based on the title only.

title: Population-Scale, Genotype-First Characterization of Monogenic Diabetes in 374,973 Individuals Across Ancestries in the NIH All of Us Research Program
summary: Using WGS from 374,973 All of Us participants (42% non-European), the authors found pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 10 MODY genes in about 1 in 1,013 people, at similar rates in European and African ancestry groups. Diabetes penetrance was incomplete (43.5% by age 60) and was highest for GCK and lowest for non-GCK/HNF genes, whose carrier risk was below that of non-carriers in the top type 2 diabetes PRS decile. Higher T2D polygenic risk further raised diabetes risk among carriers.
abstract: Current understanding of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) has been shaped by phenotype-first studies in predominantly European ancestry cohorts, leaving population-level prevalence and penetrance in a multiancestry population incompletely defined. Using a genotype-first design, we analyzed whole-genome sequencing and clinical data from 374,973 unrelated All of Us participants (42.0% non-European ancestry). We identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 10 established MODY genes and assessed carrier prevalence, diabetes penetrance, and age-dependent diabetes risk, including comparisons with noncarriers stratified by type 2 diabetes polygenic risk score (T2D PRS) and associations between T2D PRS and diabetes risk among carriers. We identified 370 carriers (0.099%; 1 in 1,013), with similar prevalence among European and African ancestry participants (0.105% in both). Diabetes penetrance was incomplete (13.4% by age 40; 43.5% by age 60) and varied by etiology: highest for GCK (56.0% by age 60), intermediate for HNF genes (HNF1A, HNF1B, and HNF4A; 45.4%), and lowest for non-GCK/HNF genes (ABCC8, INS, KCNJ11, NEUROD1, PDX1, and RFX6; 29.0%). In Cox models, carriers of variants in non-GCK/HNF genes had modestly increased diabetes risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.64; 95% CI 1.19-2.27), which was numerically lower than among noncarriers in the top 10% of T2D PRS (HR 1.91; 95% CI 1.87-1.95). Higher T2D PRS was also associated with greater diabetes risk among carriers (HR per SD 1.32; 95% CI 1.13-1.56). These findings support equitable consideration of MODY genetic testing across ancestries and highlight substantial heterogeneity in diabetes risk among carriers of pathogenic variants in MODY genes.

title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure
summary: Each RNA secondary-structure predictor has its own interface and software requirements. RNAcomp2D wraps classical thermodynamic and deep-learning predictors in containers behind one web server. Users enter a sequence or pick one from RNAcentral and compare all the predictions, and a reference structure if one exists, side by side in a single viewer.
abstract: MOTIVATION: Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. RESULTS: We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-the-art methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. AVAILABILITY: Web server is available at https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/. Data and source code are available at https://github.com/sinc-lab/RNAcomp2D. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: VEuPathDB: 2026 update on data, tools, and infrastructure for eukaryotic pathogens, vectors, and hosts
summary: VEuPathDB now holds over 2,600 datasets for more than 800 pathogen, vector and host organisms. New features include a My Datasets workspace for uploading and analysing users' own data and guided differential-expression analysis that needs no programming, and its processing pipelines now run as containerized Nextflow workflows. The update also describes how the resource kept going under a community funding model after it lost its federal grant.
abstract: The eukaryotic pathogen, vector, and host informatics resource (VEuPathDB, https://veupathdb.org) provides open access to genomic and other large-scale data for protozoan and fungal pathogens, arthropod vectors, and their hosts, supporting >800 organisms and 2602 datasets across 12 component databases, OrthoMCL, and the newly added dataExplorer, as of Release 71 (August 2026). Since our last update, 292 datasets have been integrated, gene product descriptions improved, and OrthoMCL expanded to over 819 000 orthology groups spanning 9.2 million proteins. Artificial intelligence-assisted approaches now support dataset curation, community gene annotation, and experimental summaries of transcriptomic evidence on gene pages, each subject to expert or user review. The new My Datasets workspace lets researchers upload, analyze, and share their own data alongside curated datasets, and a guided interface supports differential expression analysis without programming. Infrastructure has been consolidated from 15 Oracle databases into a single PostgreSQL platform, with data-processing pipelines migrated to containerized Nextflow workflows. This period was also defined by the loss of the long-standing US federal award that funded VEuPathDB, its temporary closure in September 2024, and its restoration under a community-supported model of voluntary tiered subscriptions, donations, and philanthropic support, with all data and tools remaining freely accessible.

title: pyGENIE: A Python library for programmatic access and mutational analysis of AACR Project GENIE
summary: Working with the huge AACR Project GENIE cancer-genomics release (>268,000 samples) usually means writing custom code around complex flat files. pyGENIE is a Python package with one API for clinical and genomic queries, tumor mutational burden and mutational-signature analysis (SigProfiler, SigMA), and it returns pandas DataFrames. In a lung adenocarcinoma case study it reproduced known mutation patterns with about ten times less code.
abstract: MOTIVATION: As of today, AACR Project GENIE has completed 19 data releases since its launch in 2015. The latest release includes more than 268 000 samples from nearly 250 000 patients, and as of February 2026, over 1730 scientific journal articles have cited Project GENIE data. Despite its scale and scientific impact, programmatic analysis of GENIE data often still requires researchers to work directly with complex flat files and develop custom data integration workflows. RESULTS: Here we present pyGENIE, a Python package that provides a unified API for accessing GENIE flat files, performing clinical and genomic queries, computing tumor mutational burden, and integrating with leading mutational signature analysis tools including SigProfiler and SigMA. Following a data-as-a-service paradigm, pyGENIE returns all results as native pandas DataFrames, enabling seamless integration with machine learning and visualization libraries. Applied to a lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) case study, pyGENIE reproduces known mutation frequencies, co-mutation patterns, and mutational signatures while reducing the required codebase by approximately an order of magnitude. AVAILABILITY: pyGENIE is freely available at https://github.com/gersteinlab/pyGENIE under the MIT License, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21981945, and can be installed from PyPI using pip install pygenie-sdk. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
